Breaking: Is the Energy Crisis Accelerating the Clean Energy Transition? 4 Takeaways from the IEA’s World Energy Outlook 2026

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1266 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Energy expert Nick Wayth unpacks findings from this year’s report—and what needs to happen next.
  • Industry observers note that the International Energy Agency has published its World Energy Outlook 2026 amid an unprecedented global energy crisis that is reshaping how countries think about energy security.
  • What do these findings mean for the energy transition, and where should policymakers focus their efforts?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Energy expert Nick Wayth unpacks findings from this year’s report—and what needs to happen next.

Industry observers note that the International Energy Agency has published its World Energy Outlook 2026 amid an unprecedented global energy crisis that is reshaping how countries think about energy security. The report finds that the push to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels is accelerating electrification and the shift toward domestic energy sources, including renewables. Yet electricity demand is surging, grids are struggling to keep pace, and concerns about energy security are also giving coal a longer life in some countries. The IEA warns that the pursuit of energy security alone won’t deliver the emissions reductions needed to meet global climate goals.

What do these findings mean for the energy transition, and where should policymakers focus their efforts? Nick Wayth, global director of the WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition, explains four key takeaways from this year’s report—and what needs to happen next.

Q: How close will current and proposed policies get us to the COP31 pledge to raise electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035? What changes are needed to bridge the gap?

According to recent reports, the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz has reinforced the case for electrification as a way for countries to diversify their power sources and reduce dependence on imports, improving energy security and affordability. While the world’s reliance on fossil fuels hasn’t changed substantially, there’s been a real shift in how countries think about the risks of that dependence—and the benefits of electrification. But progress is too slow. The IEA projects that under current and proposed policies, electricity will account for only 29% of final energy consumption by 2035. That’s only half the increase needed to reach the COP31 target of 35%.

Much of the technology is already available. The IEA estimates that nearly half of fossil fuel demand in road transport and more than a third of demand for low- and medium-temperature industrial heat could be electrified at a competitive cost today. The challenge is creating the conditions for businesses and households to make that switch.

In a recent development, to reach the target, countries need to develop detailed looks for shifting transport, heating, and heavy industry toward electricity and invest in transmission and distribution. Governments can help keep their industries competitive by making it more attractive for businesses to switch from gas to affordable electricity. Some countries are doing this successfully already. Germany, for example, has reduced electricity taxes for manufacturers and has subsidized grid charges, helping lower electricity costs for businesses.

Q: The IEA projects rapid growth in electricity demand from both air conditioning and data centers. How do the challenges posed by these two sources of demand differ?

Energy demand from AI and data centers has dominated public attention this year, but by 2035 the global growth in electricity demand from cooling is forecast to be about 70% greater than from data centers. Notably, the IEA finds that global demand for cooling buildings is overtaking demand for heating them for the first time in history.

Energy demand from data centers is concentrated in the U.S., China, and the EU. By contrast, demand for cooling is widespread, especially in emerging and developing economies where much of the population is vulnerable to extreme heat, an increasing threat to human life.

Under current and proposed government policies, cooling is projected to account for 12% of global electricity consumption by 2035. But during periods of peak demand, when millions of air conditioners are running at once, it could reach around 30% of the electricity needed. Electricity grids must be able to cope with these spikes in demand, even if they occur only occasionally. Without better planning and more efficient cooling, countries could face costly grid upgrades—or risk power outages during extreme heat.

This is why policymakers and utilities need to anticipate future electricity demand and plan investments in grid infrastructure accordingly. But building more isn’t the only solution. Governments and utilities should also invest in energy storage and other grid flexibility measures that enable them to adapt to fluctuating supply and demand as needed.

Industry observers note that Q: The energy crisis is accelerating clean electrification in some countries but also encouraging greater reliance on fossil fuels in others. What does the IEA’s outlook tell us about the future of oil, coal, and gas—and the risks of investing in new fossil fuel infrastructure?

The report highlights that global oil demand is expected to level off by 2030 under current and proposed policies. The slowdown in China’s oil demand, driven largely by electric vehicle adoption, is expected to continue. Other fast-growing economies, such as India, despite electrifying transport, are nonetheless projected to increase their demand for oil.

The current energy crisis is reinforcing these differences in strategy. Some countries are investing in electrification to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels, while others are turning to domestic fossil fuels.

The energy crisis has given coal demand a short-term boost, and the IEA now expects coal use in 2035 to be higher than it projected just a year ago. Even so, under current and proposed government policies, global coal demand is expected to fall by 14% between 2025 and 2035, driven largely by a decline in coal-fired power generation, particularly in China. But coal use in industry is projected to fall by just 5%, highlighting the challenge of reducing dependence on the fuel.

Countries need to be cautious about investing in infrastructure that may not be needed. The IEA estimates that about 400 billion cubic meters (bcm) of fresh liquefied natural gas (LNG) export capacity is under construction and could come online by 2035. Yet under current and stated government policies, export capacity could significantly exceed demand in 2035 by70 bcm. That surplus raises the risk of underused infrastructure and investments that fail to pay off.

The IEA estimates that the world will need at least 25 million kilometers of upcoming power lines over the next decade to meet growing electricity demand and connect new sources of power, including renewables. Another 15 million kilometers of existing lines will need to be upgraded or replaced. Both will require substantial investment.

The biggest challenge is delivering these changes fast enough. Major grid projects can take 5 to15 years to strategy, secure permits for, and complete—far longer than many renewable energy projects. Governments need to speed up permitting and grid connections, improve coordination between utilities and developers, and encourage investment before demand materializes. One encouraging example is the EU’s recent provisional agreement to streamline permitting for grid projects.

Equally crucial is to invest in ways to use existing assets more efficiently. Grid-enhancing technologies can speed up connections by allowing existing power lines to carry more electricity, reducing the need to build newly introduced infrastructure. And increasingly, governments and utilities are seeing the importance of making grids more flexible—building in capability and strategies to balance supply with demand in real time. Brazil, for example, pays large electricity users to temporarily reduce consumption when the grid is under strain. Businesses that fail to deliver the agreed reductions can lose payments or face suspension from programs. By combining energy storage, demand-response programs, smart grid controls, distributed energy generation, and other flexibility strategies, energy planners can meet growing demands and increase resilience while reducing the need to build more grid infrastructure.

Courtesy of WRI. By Sarah George, Senior Manager, Strategic Communications, WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition; and Francisco Boshell, Global Lead, Decarbonized Energy Consumption, WRI Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition.

Why Cars Need To Be Driven To Stay In Peak Condition

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (802 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
  • Humans anthropomorphize cars in many different and often goofy ways, but there is one thing we have in common: sedentary lifestyles are bad for both of us.
  • Of course, life happens and sometimes that extra project car that you're "definitely going to have running next week" sits for weeks, months, or even years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Humans anthropomorphize cars in many different and often goofy ways, but there is one thing we have in common: sedentary lifestyles are bad for both of us. Much like neglecting to stretch those hammies can add strain to certain movements, leaving your car untouched can cause components to seize up, and both can be a major pain in the butt. While time comes for us all and everything will eventually deteriorate from age, keeping active can still help keep us in peak shape and prevent additional concerns from arising.

Of course, life happens and sometimes that extra project car that you're "definitely going to have running next week" sits for weeks, months, or even years. However, this can have real consequences. Leaving your car stationary too long can result in brake corrosion, battery problems, fuel system issues, and leaks. All can lead to reduced performance or potentially costly repairs.

Thankfully, many of these problems can be mitigated by simply using your vehicle for what it is designed for — regular driving! Taking a weekly cruise that lasts about 20 to 30 minutes, per AAA guidance, will help keep your vehicle's fluids flowing, parts lubricated, and battery charged. Turns out, hitting those favorite back roads is actually good for both you and your car.

So what does regular driving help prevent? Well, in as little as a day or two, a thin layer of rust can form on the brake rotors of a parked car. Fortunately, this is mostly cosmetic and normal driving clears this up after a few stops, but over extended periods of time corrosion can set in and seize up braking components.

Fuel that sits in your gas tank lasts about three to six months before it starts to break down. In older cars with metal fuel tanks, condensation can collect and start to rust the tank out from the inside. Aged fuel and moisture in your fuel system can lower octane, gum up fuel injectors, and lead to reduced performance. Keeping your fuel tank full (in this economy?) and cycled through every few months will help mitigate fuel system concerns.

According to recent reports, an issue that may require immediate intervention is a weak crank or no start from a dead battery. Batteries naturally lose charge with time, and even more so depending on battery age or if there are any parasites drawing current when the vehicle is off. Additionally, cold weather reduces a battery's cranking power on top of the natural battery discharge. Routine driving helps keep your battery topped off via the alternator so your car is ready.

Industry observers note that tires and belts will eventually need replacing. You may even find a flat spot in a tire that's sitting for too long. Seals and gaskets that keep fluids in place can dry up and crack when not driven enough to keep everything conditioned, soft, and flexible, which can cause leaks throughout your vehicle's powertrain. Depending on the seal and severity of the leak, this may require repair and keep your vehicle stationary even longer.

Recent findings suggest that if you know your car is going to be sitting for a while, there are a few steps you can take to protect your car. I grew up in the Northeast, where it's common to put away the "nice" car for a few months over the winter so it doesn't get destroyed by road salt. Indoor storage is optimal for protection from the elements, but I'm no Rockefeller and my cars get parked outside.

In a recent development, the annual ritual involves topping off the tank and adding a fuel stabilizer to prevent fuel degradation. Attaching a trickle charger keeps a low current fed to the battery and helps it stay ready to go. Changing the oil prior to storage will remove contaminants from the engine as an added layer of protection. A good cleaning inside and out can keep blemishes or stains from setting in. With that prep out of the way, you should be safe to get through the season.

When the time comes to start your car after it has been sitting for a while, do a quick visual inspection. Check for underinflated or flat tires, the presence of animals, and any new leaks. If the tires are okay, fluids are at normal levels, there aren't any pools below your car or new inhabitants, and your battery isn't dead, you should be good to go. Drive it easy until the engine comes up to temp and listen for any new or unusual sounds. Just like humans, keeping your car in peak shape requires attention. Doing so will keep both you and your car happier and healthier for many more miles.

#65071. How Can Energy Improve Lives? Why Counting Connections Isn’t Enough

How Can Energy Improve Lives? Why Counting Connections Isn’t Enough

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1464 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Global tracking of energy access should expand beyond connections to include affordability, reliability, adequacy, and development outcomes.
  • Access to energy is a cornerstone of development—it can improve health, education, incomes, and overall quality of life.
  • It has been revealed that but access is only the first step.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Global tracking of energy access should expand beyond connections to include affordability, reliability, adequacy, and development outcomes.

Access to energy is a cornerstone of development—it can improve health, education, incomes, and overall quality of life.

It has been revealed that but access is only the first step. A health clinic can’t perform surgery if frequent power cuts make its equipment unreliable. An electric irrigation pump is unlikely to raise a farmer’s income if crops can’t reach buyers. And a small business may gain little from electricity if it lacks financing to buy the equipment it needs to expand.

For energy to improve people’s lives, it must be affordable, sufficient, and reliable—and people and businesses must be able to put it to productive use.

It has been revealed that the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 7 (SDG 7) calls for “universal access to affordable, reliable, and modern energy services” by 2030. But the two indicators used to track its universal-access target focus only on whether people have access to electricity and whether they primarily rely on clean fuels and technologies. They do not address reliability, affordability, or economic impacts.

Other approaches already offer a fuller picture. The World Bank’s Energy Sector Management Assistance Program developed the Multi-Tier Framework to measure electricity access beyond connections, including whether electricity is available when needed, adequate for the equipment people want to use, reliable and affordable. While the framework is used by some countries to assess these broader dimensions of energy access, such measures are not the default, as many countries rely on the U.N.’s official global indicators.

Industry observers note that as governments consider what should follow the SDGs after 2030, they should make multidimensional energy-access measures a regular part of national surveys and use the results to track progress globally. Since access alone does not necessarily deliver better livelihoods, improved measures of access could also be paired with indicators of whether energy is delivering the development outcomes it is intended to support. These could include whether clinics and schools can function as intended, farmers can increase yields and incomes and businesses can grow revenues and employment.

Together, these measures could shift energy planning from the largely supply-side question of how many people have access toward the demand-side questions of what people and institutions need energy for and whether the energy system enables them to meet these needs.

The examples below show why looking beyond connections matters in practice.

Industry observers note that national electrification rates can mask large differences in where electricity is available within a country. Addressing those gaps requires looking beyond national averages to identify the households, businesses, and public facilities that lack access.

Sources indicate that in 2023, WRI, working closely with Uganda’s Ministry of Health, used WRI’s Energy Access Explorer (EAE)—an online mapping tool that combines energy data with information on infrastructure, public services, and economic activity—to assess the electricity needs of health facilities. The analysis found that 675 facilities serving more than 3 million people had no electricity, either grid or off-grid, yet all were in areas with significant solar energy potential. The analysis helped identify places where solar power could fill the energy gap.

Sources indicate that in Ethiopia, the Ministry of Water and Energy and the World Bank used EAE to help design a financing program for off-grid electricity. The analysis identified 145 priority woredas, or districts, where investments could reach more than 19 million people. Having this location-based data helped translate national energy-access goals into decisions about where public financing should be directed.

In a recent development, ethiopia also illustrates why simple access figures can overstate the level of service people receive. A 2025 national energy-access survey found that 65% of households had access to at least one source of electricity. However, just 44% of the population received at least a basic level of electricity service, enough for uses such as lighting and charging a phone for at least four hours a day.

Simply having an electricity connection is not enough if the supply lacks the capacity or voltage stability to operate the equipment people need.

Industry observers note that in the Gumla district in Jharkhand, India, villages that had gained household grid connections still lacked enough power for many businesses to function. WRI found that the single-phase electricity supplied was insufficient for productive uses such as milling and oil pressing. Beginning in 2015, Mlinda Charitable Trust, a nonprofit, installed solar mini-grids that supplied three-phase electricity, allowing local enterprises to run equipment, including rice and wheat hullers, oil expellers, flour mills, and pulverizers.

Governments should assess not only whether communities are connected but also whether the electricity supplied can meet the capacity and power-quality requirements of the services and equipment people need—and plan grid upgrades or complementary systems accordingly.

A connection provides limited benefit if households, businesses, or public facilities cannot pay for enough energy to meet their needs. Measuring meaningful access therefore also means asking whether the energy is affordable for the people and institutions expected to use it.

In Ethiopia’s Berbere district, farmers initially used petrol-powered pumps to irrigate their fields, but high fuel and maintenance costs meant these were too expensive for many to keep using. Petrol cost $91 to $203 per hectare a year, while repairs and the cost of transporting fuel added further expenses.

According to recent reports, WRI and the Danish nonprofit DanChurchAid later installed two solar-powered pumps serving 48 farming households. The solar systems have no fuel costs, while maintenance costs are less than $10 a year, compared with more than $1,300 for petrol pumps. But the two pumps’ combined $19,200 upfront cost was beyond what most farmers could afford out of pocket. Governments and funders should therefore assess both the ongoing cost of using energy and the upfront cost of the technologies needed to use it, and provide financing or targeted support where high initial costs remain a barrier.

Recent findings suggest that being connected to the grid does not mean electricity will be available whenever it is needed. WRI researchers documented power cuts lasting three to 12 hours a day at two health facilities in Jharkhand, with outages worsening during the monsoon season. The facilities relied on diesel generators and small battery backups during outages.

In 2017, after solar photovoltaic systems and larger batteries were installed, the facilities were able to keep wards and offices running and power other essential equipment during grid outages, reducing their reliance on grid electricity.

Tracking the frequency and duration of outages would give a clearer picture of whether electricity is dependable enough to support essential services.

According to recent reports, even when energy is available, adequate, affordable, and reliable, it may not translate into better livelihoods. People also need equipment, financing, and access to markets to put energy to productive use.

In Uganda, WRI Africa and partners used EAE to identify $15 million in potential investments in renewable energy technologies, including solar-powered irrigation systems and equipment for cooling and milling, that could benefit more than 28,000 farmers. Some organizations identified through that work have since secured funding for related projects. Masaka District Farmers Association, for example, received an IKI Small Grants award for an irrigation project that equipped 150 hectares of coffee-growing land with drip irrigation and worked with 1,500 smallholder farmers.

In Berbere, solar-powered irrigation has enabled farmers to harvest three to four times a year and grow higher-value crops. In their first season, many farmers earned four to 10 times as much from onion, pepper, and cabbage sales as they had previously earned in a year from staple crops.

Tracking these outcomes alongside measures of energy access can help show whether investments are translating into higher productivity and incomes.

Making greater use of existing multidimensional measures, alongside complementary indicators of development outcomes, could change not just how governments report progress but also how they strategy and direct investment.

Rather than starting with how many newly introduced connections a project can deliver, governments and funders would ask what people and institutions need energy for, what prevents them from using it effectively, and which investments could remove those barriers. In some places, that may mean extending electricity supply. In others, it could mean improving reliability, lowering costs, or helping farmers and businesses obtain the equipment and financing needed to use energy productively.

Sources indicate that energy is essential to improving human well-being, but it is only one part of what drives development. Like water, health care or education and energy is necessary but not sufficient. Treating access as a starting point rather than an end goal—and measuring whether people can use, afford, and rely on the energy they receive—would give governments a clearer picture of whether energy investments are improving people’s lives.

Courtesy of WRI. Experts: Dimitris Mentis, Harsha Meenawat.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that while many Americans are struggling to meet their basic needs, automakers are moving further upmarket. Porsche's mid-engined Mission S supercar concept, for example, is aimed at an ultra-wealthy clientele, with an estimated $500,000 starting price for the production model. And Jay Leno has something to say about this.

It has been revealed that during an interview with TBPN on YouTube, Leno noted Porsche was "moving upscale" with the Mission S: "They want to be like Ferrari. Sell fewer cars [for] more money to fewer people." In the old days, he said, "A Ferrari had 800 miles and Porsche had 60,000. A Corvette, same thing." And back then, when people used to hold shootouts to find out which car was the fastest, "the only ones that showed up would be Corvette and Porsche. Everybody else just didn't." Nowadays, Leno continued, people "buy a GT3 and [say,] 'I'm putting it away.'" He added, "Porsches have always been expensive, but they're not rare. There's a lot of them around.".

And while Leno mentions how someone reasonably financially successful could still aspire to own a Corvette, the lineup has gone fairly upmarket, especially with the ZR1X in the mix — although the ZR1X's starting price of roughly $230,000 is considerably lower than those of most modern Ferraris and Lamborghinis, it's still a pretty expensive automobile.

Recent findings suggest that leno concluded that this strategy of selling fewer but pricier cars is spreading across the auto industry and, more broadly, the economy as a whole. "You're either Motel 6 or the Four Seasons. ... We have no middle class anymore. And that's the sad thing.".

Sources indicate that there's no official definition of the middle class, at least not one that's widely agreed upon. The Pew Research Center defines middle-income households as those with an income (adjusted for household size) that's between two-thirds and double that of the U.S. median household income. Upper-income households earn more than double the median, while lower-income households earn less than two-thirds of it. By that measure, 61% of Americans were part of the middle class in 1971, with that share dropping to 51% by 2023.

Sources indicate that in fact, the share of household income held by the middle class has fallen in almost every decade since 1970. Middle-income households held 62% of all U.S. household income in 1970, but just 43% in 2022. Upper-income households, meanwhile, saw a massive gain in their share, jumping from 29% to 48%.

The middle-class decline can also be attributed to the pace at which income grew. Inflation-adjusted incomes across all tiers improved between 1970 and 2022, but not at the same rate. Upper-income households saw 78% growth, compared with just 60% for middle-income households. Lower-income folks saw the least growth (55%). In 2024, the median income of an upper-income household was $278,800, versus $115,900 for middle-income and $38,400 for lower-income households, according to Pew's 2026 report. And while upper-income households had 6.8 times the typical income of lower-income households in 2001, that number had risen to 7.3 by 2024.

Sources indicate that it's deeply concerning how new car sales are booming for the rich and falling for everyone else. Some of our readers have shared how their finances are holding them back from buying a new car in 2026, and they are certainly not alone.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps Jay's take on the middle class being nonexistent is a bit of a stretch. But as you can tell, income inequality is real. According to the Economic Policy Institute, between 1979 and 2023, the average annual earnings of the bottom 90% of workers saw cumulative growth of 44%, while the top 0.1% posted staggering growth of 354%. Although Americans earning an hourly wage were getting bigger paychecks than in the '70s, their purchasing power had remained largely unchanged after you factor in inflation, per a 2018 study from Pew. And according to data gathered by Statista, average real wages were down 0.8% in July 2026 compared with January 2021.

According to recent reports, no wonder there's an affordability crisis. The data shows that President Trump's repeated claims of it being "fake" and a "hoax" couldn't be further from the truth, and plenty of working families can attest to that.

In a recent development, this is a nasty combination for markets. Bitcoin fell around 3.2% over 24 hours, gold futures dropped more than 3%, and WTI crude lost around 3%. It has been revealed that here’s the comparison. In March 2020, the Fed was slashing rates, buying bonds and throwing emergency liquidity at a financial system under immense pressure. Congress approved a $2.2 trillion rescue package to keep households and businesses afloat.

Today, we are watching markets fall while the Fed is possibly making money more expensive.

Industry observers note that october’s FOMC minutes weren’t exactly what markets wanted to hear. The Fed held rates at 3.75%–4% during its October meeting, but almost all participants believed further increases would likely be appropriate. Two officials also stated a hike larger than the usual 25 basis points could be considered if inflation data came in hotter than expected.

Industry observers note that and there was more in those minutes than just interest rates. Officials raised concerns about hedge fund leverage and the growing debt tied to artificial intelligence investments. Some financing arrangements could become a problem if investors start questioning enormous AI spending, and whether it will generate the returns companies expect.

In a recent development, the risk is forced selling. Leveraged funds facing losses or investor withdrawals may have to dump assets swiftly, potentially pushing prices down further.

Gold has its own problem. A stronger dollar and higher interest rates make it less attractive to investors who can earn a return elsewhere. Bitcoin price, meanwhile, remains vulnerable when traders cut exposure to speculative assets.

In a recent development, the Fed hasn’t declared a financial emergency. Its minutes actually describe the banking system as resilient. But officials are clearly paying attention to risks that could amplify a market shock.

Discover: The Best Token Presales.

March 2020 was brutal. COVID-19 lockdowns brought businesses to a standstill. Investors rushed for cash, stocks collapsed, and Bitcoin briefly slipped below $4,000 after sitting near $10,000 just weeks earlier.

In a recent development, the Federal Reserve didn’t wait around. It cut rates by 50 basis points on March 3, then delivered another 100-basis-point cut on March 15. The federal funds target range dropped to 0%–0.25%.

On March 23, the Fed confirmed unlimited purchases of Treasury securities and mortgage-backed securities, promising to buy whatever amounts were necessary to support market functioning. It also introduced emergency lending programmes to keep credit flowing.

President Donald Trump signed the $2.2 trillion CARES Act on March 27. The package included direct payments to eligible Americans, expanded unemployment benefits, and assistance for businesses struggling to survive lockdowns. The Paycheck Protection Program gave small businesses access to loans designed to help them keep employees on payroll.

The response was enormous, but the economy was facing an extraordinary shutdown. Millions of Americans had lost their jobs, businesses were closing, and normal economic activity had practically disappeared.

Markets eventually bounced back. The S&P 500 recovered its pre-pandemic record by August 2020. Bitcoin climbed above $12,000 during the same month.

In a recent development, the current US economy isn’t in the same position as it was during the pandemic. Inflation remains above the Fed’s 2% target, and policymakers are discussing rate increases rather than cuts.

Slashing rates to zero and flooding markets with liquidity might help asset prices. It could also make inflation worse. Another multitrillion-dollar spending package would face an entirely different argument in Congress, especially without a pandemic-style economic shutdown.

The Fed doesn’t have to choose between doing nothing and repeating the 2020 rescue. If banks struggle to fund themselves or credit markets start freezing, it can step in with emergency lending and liquidity operations. That’s a much narrower response than another round of unlimited bond purchases.

It has been revealed that the Fed’s concerns about leveraged hedge funds and AI financing could become more relevant if investors start selling indiscriminately. A market correction is one thing. Forced selling spreading through the financial system is another.

Recent findings suggest that at the moment, there’s no evidence that we’re facing another March 2020. The banking system remains resilient, and falling Bitcoin prices alone won’t trigger a government bailout.

But the Fed has a problem that didn’t exist in quite the same way during the pandemic. It may need to protect financial stability without giving up its fight against inflation. In 2020, Washington opened the taps. This time, we wait and see, and Bitcoin price will survive.

What Are Drivers Supposed To Do When Encountering A 'Narrows' Road Sign?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Road signs are short, sweet, and sometimes downright goofy.
  • It has been revealed that various warning signs are used for narrowing roadways.
  • According to recent reports, the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD), which is managed by the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Road signs are short, sweet, and sometimes downright goofy. However, they're not always easy to understand. When a picture is worth a thousand words, deciphering signage with diagonal black-and-yellow stripes or arrows pointing in opposite directions is akin to playing Pictionary with toddlers: what is that shape supposed to mean?! Adding a few words can create even more ambiguity, like Pennsylvania's contribution to the worst road signs list. Which brings us to the narrows.

It has been revealed that various warning signs are used for narrowing roadways. The self-explanatory ones are emblazoned with the phrases "road narrows" and "narrow bridge." Less informative is the pictorial variation featuring an hourglass-like outline that may or may not be accompanied by vertical dashes down the middle — the figure's "hips" reference the road narrowing. Regardless of which version you see, the rules of engagement remain the same: proceed with caution.

According to recent reports, the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD), which is managed by the U.S. DOT's Federal Highway Administration (FHWA), sets the standards for all traffic-flow-related communications, including road markings, signs, and signals. Per the MUTCD, Road Narrows signs are part of the W5 series, which includes cautions for underpasses. Standardized to be yellow, warning signs will vary in shape. For the W5s, the MUTCD settled on a diamond.

In a recent development, you'll also find them only in specific places. Plenty of driving lanes narrow and widen, but only when the path is shrunk to a certain width will you come across a W5 sign. The exception is low-volume local streets with speed limits of 30 mph or less. At those speeds, you're likely able to see oncoming traffic.

It has been revealed that according to the MUTCD, a road's width must diminish so abruptly and sharply that opposing traffic cannot simultaneously pass at posted speed limits. For bridges, culverts, and underpasses, warnings are issued following the surface-street rules, as well as when the two-way road's clearance is 16 to 18 feet across. This measurement includes the shoulder, if there is one.

The guidance suggests warnings be posted roughly 155 to 325 feet ahead of narrowings in 25 mph sections and up to 990 feet in 55 mph sectors. If visibility is impaired due to curves or grades, those distances can be adjusted. In construction zones, especially dangerous highway work, the W5s switch to work-zone orange and should appear prior to lane tapers, while a second reminder can be placed closer to the work area.

Sources indicate that so, what should you do when you see a narrows sign? Because it's not a road closure and the number of lanes can be unchanged, you simply continue on. Just keep your vehicle centered and take things slow and easy, especially if there's oncoming traffic. If a large vehicle approaches, like a bus or truck, consider yielding and letting it through. Room to pass will be limited, even if there is a shoulder.

On bridges, stick to your side of the road, reduce your speed, and definitely watch out for outside mirrors. If the bridge is too narrow for two vehicles, the rule of thumb is whoever arrives first gets dibs. If there's no room, there's no point in forcing your way through. Although these signs don't say how long the road narrows, the early heads-up gives you time to prepare.

Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, Volkswagen is marking the 50th anniversary of the GTI by showing how uncompromising an electric GTI with motorsport ambitions can be. The concept car will be presented to the public next week at the Essen Motor Show (27 November to 6 December 2026). Its performance figures meet a two-door silhouette and flared wings as well as a large front splitter, diffuser and rear wing. The result: a powerful appearance and maximum downforce for fast laps. At the same time, the concept vehicle provides a preview of how the GTI idea can be further developed in the electric age.

It has been revealed that kai Grünitz, Member of the Board of Management for Technical Development, Volkswagen Brand and Brand Group Core: “The GTI has been one of Volkswagen’s great success stories for 50 years. This year, we launched our GTI as an electric vehicle in series production for the first time. With the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, we are showing how much more potential there is in the electric GTI world. Our platform strategy and MEB+ give us the technological freedom to make even extreme concepts possible.”.

In a recent development, designed for performance. The design of the new ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept is based on the production model, the 166 kW (226 PS) ID. Polo GTI. In both models, the drive power is transmitted to the front axle. In the 270 kW (367 PS) ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, this power delivery is controlled – thanks in part to an electronically regulated front differential lock (VAQ) – so that the model reaches 100 km/h from a standstill in just 4.7 seconds with Launch Control. Like the drive system, the electrical infrastructure has also been adapted to the high performance of the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept. The 52 kWh high-voltage battery can provide up to 290 kW at short notice, enabling a top speed of 240 km/h. The DCC (adaptive chassis control) has also been tuned for use on the racetrack and ensures precise handling and high traction in conjunction with the front differential lock. The new ceramic brakes of the one-box brake system are also designed for high performance.

Sources indicate that dynamics are visible in the design. On the exterior, the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept follows the powerful clarity of the ID. Polo GTI production model, while at the same time incorporating design elements that underline the motorsport characteristics. Particularly striking features are the two-door instead of four-door silhouette, pronounced flaring of the wings by 50 millimetres in each case, a large motorsport splitter at the front, a wider rear end, a new diffuser and a rear wing in carbon fibre that protrudes above the roof line.

It has been revealed that two-seater. Reduced to racing. The interior is also tailored to the racetrack, and only the basic layout of the overall cockpit has been adopted from the production model. This means there is no infotainment system, for example. The focus is solely on ergonomics and driving. The driver and front passenger sit on Recaro racing bucket seats with red 5-point harnesses. The rear and luggage compartment have been completely cleared. Instead of a rear seat system, a rollover bar painted in the GTI colour Tornado Red is integrated above and behind the front seats. The dash panel, side trims and many other details are covered in dark ArtVelours microfibre fabric with red topstitching – work that has been carried out with great precision by Volkswagen trainees. In many areas – in keeping with Volkswagen tradition – the young employees were directly involved in realisation of the concept vehicle by the Development department and designers.

Sources indicate that 550 instead of 290 newton-metres. The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept features the high-torque APP550 motor. The special technical challenge here: this motor is actually intended for the rear of large models such as the ID. Tiguan or ID.7. It therefore had to be fitted into the smaller ID. Polo as front-wheel drive and additionally combined with an electronic front differential lock. Thomas Schmall, Member of the Board of Management Volkswagen AG for Technology, and CEO of Volkswagen Group Components: “The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept highlights just how emotive electric mobility can be: This is made possible by our APP550, one of the most efficient electric drives in its class. Manufactured over one million times at the Group Components plant in Kassel, this drive was actually developed for larger vehicle classes. Integrating it into the Polo required millimetre precision and is a powerful example of engineering skill and teamwork at Volkswagen, from Development and Design through to our trainees who worked on the project.”.

GTI from the master of modular platforms. The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept is based on the modular electric drive (MEB+) platform with front-wheel drive. The result is the most dynamic interpretation of a front-wheel drive ID. model to date. At the other end of the scale is the Mission Efficiency, which is also based on the ID. Polo and set four world records as a particularly efficient near-production electric vehicle. Both concept vehicles show the large bandwidth offered by electric drive systems from maximum sportiness to outstanding efficiency.

2026 is the year of the GTI. Following the Golf GTI EDITION 50, the upcoming ID.3 GTI (sales start early 2027) and the new ID. Polo GTI (available to order since October), the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept is making its debut this year as the fourth new model under the umbrella of the iconic GTI product brand. No other compact sports car family has been as successful worldwide for half a century now – with more than 2.5 million units sold – as the GTI models.

energyRe Will Continue as Construction Manager Through Commercial Operation; Sale Reflects Strength of the Company’s South Carolina Development Platform; Transaction Expected to Close in First Quarter of 2027.

energyRe today unveiled that it has agreed to sell 100% of a portfolio of utility-scale solar projects in South Carolina to Enel Green Power North America, Inc. (EGPNA). The projects have a combined total capacity of roughly 317 MWdc of upcoming generating capacity across the Palmetto State. The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to customary conditions, including required U.S. regulatory approvals.

In a recent development, “This transaction is a strong validation of the projects we have built in South Carolina and of the team that developed them,” said Ryan Brown, Chief Operating Officer at energyRe. “Enel Green Power is a world-class owner and operator, and we are pleased to hand these projects to a partner that shares our commitment to delivering reliable, affordable power to South Carolina homes and businesses. Our team will remain on the ground as construction manager to see these projects through to commercial operation.”.

As part of the transaction, energyRe will continue to serve as construction manager through commercial operation.

energyRe has broken ground on approximately 450 MW in the last year and has nearly 700 MW in operation or late-stage development. The company’s 1.8+ GW portfolio spans 20 projects in South Carolina, North Carolina, Nebraska, and Oklahoma.

6 Fuel-Sipping Motorcycles That Will Make Your Commute Less Exorbitant

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The skyward surge in gas prices in 2026 has hit our wallets pretty hard, even more so for those who commute within city limits.
  • Recent findings suggest that these are manufacturer-claimed figures, of course, but they should still translate to some pretty awesome mileage in the real world, which can help ease your concerns regarding gas prices.
  • Kicking things off is the WR125R, which, at $3,999 (plus a $400 destination fee), is the most affordable street-legal motorcycle Yamaha offers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The skyward surge in gas prices in 2026 has hit our wallets pretty hard, even more so for those who commute within city limits. And if you use a gas-guzzling sportbike or a heavyweight cruiser to get around town, things are likely even worse for you. Fear not, though, as we've compiled a list of six commuter motorcycles currently on sale (spoiler alert: the overwhelming majority of them are Hondas), all of which claim impressively high fuel efficiency figures — specifically, more than 100 miles per gallon.

Recent findings suggest that these are manufacturer-claimed figures, of course, but they should still translate to some pretty awesome mileage in the real world, which can help ease your concerns regarding gas prices. What's also great about these motorcycles is that they're very affordably priced. However, don't expect scintillating performance out of them, as they're powered by small-capacity single-cylinder engines. Consequently, these motorcycles are best suited to urban commuting rather than zipping down a highway or freeway. That noted, some of them are dual-sport bikes, which means you can take them to off-road trails on the weekends, if you're into that.

Kicking things off is the WR125R, which, at $3,999 (plus a $400 destination fee), is the most affordable street-legal motorcycle Yamaha offers. The WR125R comes with a 125 cc single-cylinder fuel-injected motor that's liquid-cooled (the only liquid-cooled engine on this list) and develops 14 hp and 8.3 lb-ft of torque, which go to the rear wheel through a six-speed wet-clutch gearbox. Yamaha touts an estimated fuel economy of 105 mpg for the WR125R, and the bike features a 2.1-gallon fuel tank, with Yamaha quoting a maximum range of around 200 miles.

Pretty good for a city commuter, right? It doesn't end there, though, as the WR125R is a dual-sport motorcycle. As part of its off-road trappings, the WR125R packs a 41mm (1.6-inch) KYB front fork with 8.5 inches of travel, a linked-type rear Monocross shock with 7.3 inches of travel, and a generous 9.4 inches of ground clearance — all of which can make for a fun ride off the beaten path. At 304 pounds (wet), the WR125R's weight should be easy to manage for rookie riders, though some may find the 34.4-inch seat height on the taller side.

According to recent reports, priced at $2,199 (plus a $300 destination fee), the cute Honda Navi is the most affordable motorcycle on this list. The word "motorcycle" does do a bit of heavy lifting here, as the Navi's styling features a dose of scooter influence. Within its chassis sits a 109 cc single-cylinder engine that uses a carburetor, which is simple and easy to repair, but prone to hard starting in colder weather. The engine is also air-cooled instead of liquid-cooled, so it can run hot during long traffic halts.

Industry observers note that the Navi makes an estimated 8 hp and 6.5 lb-ft of torque, which is ample for trundling around city blocks at leisurely speeds. Notably, it remains the cheapest new major-brand motorcycle you can buy with an automatic gearbox, specifically a CVT, which furthers the case for the Navi being an ideal city bike. It also weighs just 234 pounds and has a 30-inch seat height, so beginners can get to grips with it promptly. However, Honda has fitted the bike with a teeny-tiny 0.9-gallon fuel tank, so at Honda's claimed 110 mpg, the range works out to around 100 miles. The Navi, therefore, is best suited for those who have short daily commutes.

It has been revealed that like the Yamaha WR125R, the XR150L is Honda's entry-level dual-sport motorcycle, priced at $3,399 (plus a $300 destination fee). It's powered by a 149 cc single-cylinder engine, which is carbureted and air-cooled, and makes 12.6 hp and 9.6 lb-ft of torque. A five-speed manual gearbox transmits that grunt to the rear wheel. As for fuel efficiency, the XR150L is quite a step above the WR125R, and even the smaller-engined Navi. Honda's figures work out to 124 mpg, and the bike offers a 2.8-gallon fuel tank — the largest-capacity tank on this list.

In a recent development, so, even though the XR150L doesn't tout the highest fuel efficiency here, its relatively massive tank enables a claimed range of 346 miles on a single tank. If your commute is on the longer side, this is the motorcycle to go for. Since it's a dual-sport bike, the XR150L additionally features a 31mm (1.22-inch) front fork with 7.1 inches of travel, a single rear shock with 5.9 inches of travel, and 9.6 inches of ground clearance. While the wheel travel is shorter than that offered by the WR125R, the XR150L has more ground clearance, and, at 282 pounds, is a decent bit lighter too. Its seat height is also noticeably lower (32.8 inches), which can make mounting and dismounting easier.

If you find yourself less interested in dual-sport bikes and motorcycle-scooter hybrids, and lean more toward retro-inspired styling, the Honda Trail125 might just be the bike for you. Priced at $4,199 (plus a $300 destination fee), the Trail125 features a distinctive design that draws on Honda's trail-bike heritage, with a high-mounted exhaust, a step-through steel backbone chassis, a rear luggage rack, and spoked wheels. The Trail125 comes fitted with a 124 cc fuel-injected single-cylinder engine that's air-cooled and produces 9 hp and 8.1 lb-ft of torque.

Sources indicate that A four-speed semi-automatic transmission — meaning you never have to work a clutch lever — is equipped as standard, and the fuel tank measures 1.4 gallons, which translates to nearly 220 miles between fill-ups, at about 157 mpg. The seat height is 31.5 inches, which is slightly taller than that of the Navi, and the Trail125 weighs 256 pounds, making it heavier than the Navi as well.

In a recent development, honda's quirkily named Grom is yet another small and cute motorcycle. It's powered by a 124 cc fuel-injected single-cylinder motor that's air-cooled and belts out nearly 10 hp and 7.7 lb-ft of torque, which go to the rear wheel via a five-speed manual gearbox. The Grom is rated for a stellar fuel economy of 161 mpg, and its 1.6-gallon fuel tank means that it can theoretically cover 257 miles before needing a refill.

The Grom is styled much like a downsized conventional motorcycle, so if you're not a fan of the Navi's scooter-like look or the XR150L's dual-sport design, it would likely appeal to you. It also weighs 224 pounds, making it lighter than the Navi, and it even matches the Navi's 30-inch seat height. As for price, the Grom is available in three trim levels, namely the Base ($3,599), SP ($3,699), and ABS ($3,799) — all three carry a destination fee of $300. The Base and SP trims are differentiated by color and graphics (the SP comes solely in a black finish, while the Base trim is offered in red, white, and blue), and the aptly named ABS trim adds front-wheel ABS.

In a recent development, taking the top spot on this list is the Monkey — one more whimsically named motorcycle from Honda. Much like the Trail125, the Monkey is a retro-inspired motorcycle, but instead of a trail bike, it resembles an old-school scrambler. Pretty cool, right? As for mechanicals, the Monkey comes equipped with a 124 cc fuel-injected single-cylinder mill that uses air cooling and develops all of 9 hp and 8 lb-ft of torque, which go to the rear wheel via a five-speed manual transmission.

Recent findings suggest that despite the Monkey's impressive 163-mpg claimed fuel economy, its 1.5-gallon fuel tank is good for around 244 miles — less than the Grom's. The seat height is also a tiny bit higher at 30.5 inches, and, at 231 pounds, the Monkey is a few pounds heavier than the Grom too. That mentioned, the Monkey does come with front-wheel ABS as standard. As for the price, the Monkey is available for $4,399 (plus a $300 destination fee), making it the most expensive motorcycle here.

Sources indicate that navigating the world of Google Ads can be challenging, especially in an industry as competitive as real estate. One term you've probably heard in relation to Google Ads is "Quality Score." This score is crucial to how your ads perform and how much they cost. But what does it mean for realtors, and what constitutes a great Google Quality Real Estate Score? Let's dive in.

Sources indicate that google Ads Quality Score is essentially a measurement of the quality and relevance of both your keywords and PPC ads. It is a dynamic metric, assigned on a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the best possible score. It is used by Google to determine your cost per click (CPC) and your ad rank in the ad auction process.

Quality Score is calculated based on three primary components: click-through rate (CTR), ad relevance, and landing page experience.

For any industry, including real estate, a good Quality Score is generally around 7 or above. However, in the competitive world of real estate, striving for an even higher Quality Score could give you an advantage. So, for realtors, a great Quality Score might be considered 8 or above.

In a recent development, that said, keep in mind that a high-Quality Score is not an end in itself. It's a sign that your ads are relevant, and your landing pages provide a good user experience, but it's still just one factor in the overall success of your Google Ads campaigns.

A high-Quality Score is beneficial for several reasons:.

Industry observers note that improving your Quality Score is all about relevance and user experience. Here are some strategies:.

Recent findings suggest that A high Google Ads Quality Score can be a strong asset for realtors. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, JJA ESS has released its own battery passport data platform to support lifecycle information management and help companies prepare for upcoming EU regulations.
  • It has been revealed that according to the EU Battery Regulation, from February 18, 2027, battery passports are mandatory for batteries used in light vehicles (LMTs), electric vehicles, and industrial batteries with a capacity exceeding 2 kWh that are placed on the market or put into service.
  • A battery passport is a digital data record linked to a single physical battery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, JJA ESS has released its own battery passport data platform to support lifecycle information management and help companies prepare for upcoming EU regulations. The platform is hosted in the company’s own cloud environment, giving the team direct responsibility for data policies, access permissions, and future updates.

It has been revealed that according to the EU Battery Regulation, from February 18, 2027, battery passports are mandatory for batteries used in light vehicles (LMTs), electric vehicles, and industrial batteries with a capacity exceeding 2 kWh that are placed on the market or put into service. Further requirements will follow.

A battery passport is a digital data record linked to a single physical battery. A QR code and a unique identifier based on the ISO/IEC 15459 series connect the data record to the battery, enabling access to information throughout its entire lifecycle. This can include product identity, material composition, CO₂ footprint, recycled content, performance and durability, condition, supply chain due diligence, and end-of-life disposal. Taken together, these data points support consistent information management from product identification to the end of the product lifecycle.

For manufacturers, the challenge lies not simply in creating a QR code. The data must be traceable back to its source, up-to-date, and accessible in accordance with regulatory and business requirements. Companies must also manage access to sensitive information and comply with regulations governing cross-border data transfers and trade secrets. This balance is particularly relevant for companies operating in multiple markets. When companies utilize a third-party platform, its functionality, access to data fields, and interoperability can be determined by the provider’s configuration and service model.

JA ESS developed the platform internally and hosts it in its own cloud environment. Data policies, access permissions, and future platform updates are managed by the JA ESS internal team. This team ensures compliance with EU regulations regarding data access, presentation, and updates, while also giving JA ESS greater control over data management. The platform can also evolve as regulatory requirements change and real-world applications provide further insights.

In a recent development, JA ESS is the energy storage business unit under the JA brand. As a central component of JA’s energy storage strategy, JA ESS offers a wide range of FTM and BTM applications with safe, efficient, intelligent, and customized solutions for the large-scale, commercial, and industrial sectors as well as the residential market.

#65059. Flock Cameras Now Have Their Eye On Students, With Hundreds Of Thousands Under Surveillance

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (737 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

Flock Cameras Now Have Their Eye On Students, With Hundreds Of Thousands Under Surveillance

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that over the last few years, Flock cameras and other AI-powered automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) have steadily spread across the United States, and until recently, the spread was relatively silent.
  • Sources indicate that over 100 public school systems have let Flock Safety expand its private spy network onto their campuses, according to The 74, leaving hundreds of thousands of students nationwide surveilled without their consent.
  • Industry observers note that if having your kids being spied on from the moment they enter the campus isn't concerning enough, there's also Flock Safety's track record to worry about.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that over the last few years, Flock cameras and other AI-powered automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) have steadily spread across the United States, and until recently, the spread was relatively silent. Today, Flock Safety has over 145,000 cameras deployed throughout the nation, though their prevalence hasn't made the public any safer. And it's not just major roads being spied on and license plates being tracked.

Sources indicate that over 100 public school systems have let Flock Safety expand its private spy network onto their campuses, according to The 74, leaving hundreds of thousands of students nationwide surveilled without their consent. This is affecting students of all ages, too. Some 150 colleges and universities have introduced mass surveillance to their campuses through Flock cameras, too, per Policing and Society: An International Journal of Research and Policy.

Industry observers note that if having your kids being spied on from the moment they enter the campus isn't concerning enough, there's also Flock Safety's track record to worry about. Flock cameras are notoriously easy to hack, and they collect an absurd amount of information, some of which lives unencrypted on the camera itself. In the past, Flock cameras have even been caught streaming on the open web, according to a report by 404Media.

One question when looking at how many schools are targeted by Flock cameras may be, "Why?" Flock says its cameras "help communities deter crime, respond to emergencies, and investigate safety incidents." And law enforcement is supposed to use Flock data to help solve crime and aid investigations. But Flock cameras also have huge abuse potential, even beyond their numerous security issues. We know that cops are looking up stuff on Flock and putting "LMAO," "WEIRD KID," and "sexy" as reasons for the searches, and we know that in Georgia alone, 17 cops have been arrested for using Flock to stalk civilians.

We also know Flock info isn't entirely accurate and has led to the detention of auto journalists, wrong cars being towed, and traffic stops and tickets based on incorrect information. Couple that with Flock Safety's attempt to shut down DeFlock, a website that maps Flock camera's in public, and the fact that police don't like Flock-inspired cameras tracking their own movements, and the intent behind installing Flock cameras at schools seems less altruistic than the marketing material might suggest. Surprise.

According to recent reports, what ALPRs at schools definitively can do is build and deepen profiles on cars that frequent the area, namely those driven by parents and students. And while Flock Safety claims that its cameras aren't capable of tracking people (or cars, for that matter), a recent hack of a Flock camera revealed that the cameras do at least detect people and save images of them. Some have rightfully voiced concerns over the privacy concerns this presents near schools and questioned how accessible this information becomes once it's on Flock's servers.

According to recent reports, after public and student pushback, some schools are canceling their Flock contracts and removing the offending cameras. Take the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee, which canceled its contract in September and called for Flock to remove the tech giant's 20-plus cameras from campus. This came on the heels of two other UW schools discontinuing their use of Flock cameras.

This is part of a bigger trend of cities across the country dumping Flock en masse, and hopefully this trend continues to spread until not just Flock, but also Axon and all other privately owned cameras are off the streets. Or at least well-regulated enough to not threaten massive security risks, and not give police warrantless access to the public's data.

For now, though, the unfortunate reality is that canceling a Flock contract doesn't necessarily remove the glitch, and it certainly doesn't undo damage already done. See, like many stalkers and creeps out there, Flock refuses to take no for an answer. The firm doesn't always remove cameras after a contract ends, sometimes opting to keep them in service instead. Some officials have taken to removing the cameras themselves, while other discontinued Flock cameras are covered with garbage bags after contract termination.

Until the cameras are actually fully removed, there's no guarantee that they're not continuing to collect data still. Maybe if we're lucky, Republican U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie's anti-Flock bill will ban automated traffic enforcement and we won't have to worry about this mess anymore.

#65055. Why Automakers Call Their Early Prototype Cars Mules

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (871 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

Why Automakers Call Their Early Prototype Cars Mules

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The hybrid equine offspring of a male donkey and a female horse is known as a mule.
  • Recent findings suggest that surely you're familiar with the concept of a pre-production development car, and you'll likely have seen some of these cars wearing heavy camouflage in spy photography over the years.
  • Industry observers note that you may recall that Porsche cobbled some 911 bodywork around the hybrid drivetrain of a 918 Spyder back in 2012.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The hybrid equine offspring of a male donkey and a female horse is known as a mule. These animals have traditionally been useful pack animals and beasts of burden because they tend to be larger, stronger, and faster than a donkey, while tougher and able to endure longer days than a horse. Because mules are typically sterile, they almost always represent the end of their bloodline. Many of these attributes also apply to pre-production cars, which might explain why they're frequently known as "test mules.".

Recent findings suggest that surely you're familiar with the concept of a pre-production development car, and you'll likely have seen some of these cars wearing heavy camouflage in spy photography over the years. Automakers use these pre-production testers to help develop the driving and chassis dynamics and guide them through the parts-selection process. Usually they're used in the development of new hardware, whether that be a new engine, early electric motor prototyping, or a new suspension design. They are often cobbled together from existing componentry, and hidden under the skin of an existing production car in an effort to hide their true intent.

Industry observers note that you may recall that Porsche cobbled some 911 bodywork around the hybrid drivetrain of a 918 Spyder back in 2012. That thing looked weird. Or maybe you remember the extra-long-wheelbase 348 Ferrari used to develop the now-iconic Enzo. Another favorite is the Holden Maloo ute Chevrolet imported from Australia to use as a development chassis for the mid-engine C8 Corvette, stuffing that V8 right in the truck bed (photo below). There are thousands of slightly less exciting examples, of course.

Sources indicate that before a vehicle reaches production, automakers have to spend thousands of hours and miles making sure the components are up to snuff. Sometimes these cars are used for years ahead of their scheduled production manufacture, letting engineers make changes on the fly in the development phase. Sometimes these mules end up going nowhere, as the engineers figure out their ideas weren't viable. Sometimes they're used for final validation of simple things like weight distribution, or setting ride and handling tweaks.

Sources indicate that like the animal mule, automotive mules are frequently hybrids of a few different cars, keeping costs down by using stuff automakers already have in the parts bin. The word has frequently been used to allude to anything made in a hybrid manner. Additionally, like the mule, these are cars that are putting in the work for the organization. They may be philosophically sterile, never to produce offspring, but they can help move the heavy load of getting a car closer to production. Perhaps that's why these cars have been dubbed "mule.".

However, pre-production prototype mules are likely called that because of the role of a mule car in motorsport. Italian race teams frequently referred to their spare or test cars as "mulettos" or little mules (also a slang term for forklifts in Italian). Here's a brief explanation from Pirelli Tires: "It originates from the 1930s, when cars that were used for training racing drivers or testing newly introduced parts needed to be strong and reliable rather than necessarily fast: a bit like mules, especially when contrasted with the capricious thoroughbreds that were the actual race cars.".

After decades of use in motorsport, the concept of a test car being called a mule seems to have spread to the road car engineers as well.

It has been revealed that consider, for a moment, this rather innocuous looking 1980s Ford Transit van. You probably wouldn't suspect from the outside that this is effectively a test bed for Jaguar's exciting 542-horsepower XJ220 supercar. That's exactly what it is, though. Right in the middle of the white van's load floor is the 3.5-liter Tom Walkinshaw Racing-built twin-turbo V6 cribbed directly from TWR's Jaguar racing program. In an effort to quickly work out all the bugs in the XJ220's drivetrain, Jaguar engineers slapped this van together.

Sources indicate that the story goes that Jaguar not only could get plenty of road testing miles on the engine without attracting much attention, but could also position an engineer in the back of the van to directly monitor the engine while it was driving, tuning for turbo lag and the like. In an effort to disguise the van further and convince passersby that it was just a regular white van, Jag engineers put newspapers and candy wrappers on the dashboard to make it look like the work vehicle of a plumber or construction worker.

According to recent reports, perhaps I don't speak for everyone when I say this, but I believe this test van is perhaps even cooler than the XJ220 that it muled for. To get an XJ220, you merely had to be a wealthy person in the late 1980s, but this van has a story, and stories are what make cars cool. I feel the same about pre-production prototypes of pretty much any supercar ever made. There's an engineered necessity here that makes the prototype cooler. Mules are just plain cooler than the horses or the donkeys they're derived from — it's a real "the whole is greater than the sum of its parts" situation.

#65054. Why Do Empty-Nest Boomers Own So Many Homes in Top School Districts?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (961 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Realtor ↗ Open Full Page

Why Do Empty-Nest Boomers Own So Many Homes in Top School Districts?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (961 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best-performing school districts often bring stiff competition from families looking to break in, while older neighbors stay put.
  • The paper from the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland studied the household characteristics of the best-performing school districts in the country, which command higher real estate prices but also a higher barrier to entry.
  • The Cleveland Fed's findings show that seniors occupy a larger share of households in good school districts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best-performing school districts often bring stiff competition from families looking to break in, while older neighbors stay put. But helping free up housing in these districts isn't as simple as getting older people to move, a new study argues.

The paper from the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland studied the household characteristics of the best-performing school districts in the country, which command higher real estate prices but also a higher barrier to entry.

The Cleveland Fed's findings show that seniors occupy a larger share of households in good school districts. But it pinned that on affordability challenges. Higher-income households of all types compete for housing in the best-performing school districts.

Industry observers note that this is a conundrum for neighborhoods. Seniors are thus left in neighborhoods paying premiums for school districts they don't use. Meanwhile young families who'd like move into the district face limited options for homes there.

Of course, many seniors want to age in place in homes that they've lived in for decades. But others looking to downsize are "locked in" due to high mortgage rates. That can leave them in homes that they can't afford or, worse, in homes that pose safety risks for aging people.

"These findings suggest that policies aimed solely at encouraging older households to downsize are unlikely to substantially improve access to quality school districts," the paper says.

Low housing turnover in these districts drives up prices. The higher-rated public school districts are, on average, 49% more expensive, and homes there move faster, Realtor.com® data highlights. But in some of the nation's top school districts—including in Dallas, Los Angeles, and San Fransisco—homes can sell for three times the price of surrounding metros.

Using data from the American Community Survey, the Cleveland Fed found that households over 65 occupy a disproportionate share of the housing stock in the best-performing school districts. While these account for 26.2% of all households nationally, they make up as much as 28.7% of households in the least affordable areas.

Industry observers note that meanwhile households with children, which make up about 31.2% of U.S. households, occupy 30.1% of housing in the best school districts and 40% of the housing stock in the lowest-quality districts. The same doesn't ring true for one-person households, which tend to be more evenly distributed.

Older homeowners move at about the same rate across all school districts—about 6.9% a year. About 81% of older adults in the best school districts own their homes. To the Cleveland Fed, that demonstrates older households aren't limiting turnover of housing stock in high-quality and high-cost districts.

"While older households occupy a modestly larger share of housing in these expensive, high-quality areas, they do not appear to limit turnover," the paper states. "These patterns suggest that the challenge of accessing high-quality school districts is driven by a combination of income sorting and competition from multiple household types rather than solely by empty-nesters’ aging in place.".

Sources indicate that realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu notes a few problems are affecting seniors as they consider their futures. They include capital gains taxes they'd incur on homes that have appreciated in value. They also include the kinds of taxes they'd incur when they move to a upcoming place. Then there are the social considerations.

According to recent reports, "Right-sized, single-level, accessible homes near family and doctors are scarce," Xu states. "Moving also means leaving behind the neighbors and community that owners have built over decades. For many longtime owners, there are few good places to go.".

According to recent reports, buyers can still find deals in some of these good markets, Realtor.com found, if they look carefully. But in some good districts, there simply aren't a lot of homes changing hands.

Xu adds that she's surprised that young professionals without children can also compete for housing in these expensive districts. Jobs, urban amenities, and investment opportunity for the real estate tend to make these areas attractive.

"Even if more seniors moved, the homes they left would likely go to higher-income buyers, because this is a sorting story. The districts wouldn’t become much more affordable," Xu says. "The more direct solution is building more homes in and near high-demand districts. Adding right-sized options could also give older owners who want to move somewhere to go, but supply is what would ease pressure on prices.".

To Arick Morton, CEO of NIC MAP, the frozen market points to a need for more housing oriented toward seniors. Earlier this year, his group noted the nation needs to add 1 million new senior housing units by 2040. That $1 trillion homebuilding frenzy would meet the moment 10 million baby boomers pass age 80.

"People stay at home much longer than they did previously," Morton remarked. "Of course folks stay at home as long as they can and then movie into senior housing when the need is there.".

But when there isn't enough senior housing or they don't have good alternatives to downsize, those seniors end up displaced when age or an accident means they require more intensive care needs.

Recent findings suggest that "The best policy options are those that help expedite the construction of senior housing," Morton stated. "We don't have enough capacity to create a dent in that logjam.".

He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, waymo has apparently run into some problems with its robotaxis on highways in California, and it has pulled its robotaxis off of highways across the United States as a result. The main issue is that Waymo robotaxis have entered active construction zones. (Yikes!).

Sources indicate that earlier this week, in response to the Waymo vehicles driving into active construction zones, California required that Waymo stop operating its robotaxis on highways for the time being. Following that, the firm also decided to pause highway operation anywhere in the USA.

According to recent reports, “The closed freeway lanes recall stems from unusual circumstances where a Waymo vehicle may enter and ​continue driving in a closed freeway lane, the company noted, adding it is still working ​on the recall remedy. Waymo said there were no collisions or injuries reported from the closed freeway events,” Reuters reports.

According to recent reports, in addition to the above issues, Waymo robotaxis have not operated appropriately at times when manual traffic control has replaced traffic lights. Waymo issued an revision recently following a crash that occurred as a result of this problem. “The ‌manual ⁠traffic recall is to ensure self-driving vehicles better responds to manual commands at intersections from law enforcement or other emergency personnel and follows a collision in which a Waymo followed directions from an officer, but the officer was then temporarily obstructed. That update was completed on November 6.”.

Recent findings suggest that so, yes, Waymo robotaxis still aren’t perfect. However, Waymo continues to point out that its vehicles are much safer statistically than human-driven vehicles, as these vehicles are traveling far more miles between accidents than average human American drivers.
