📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you're into cars, it's basically common knowledge at this point that both Yamahas — the two independent companies that make musical instruments and motorbikes – helped put engines into several brands' cars. Yamaha also helped Lexus out when it came to making the LFA's engine sound just right and aided in creating that car's ancestor, the Toyota 2000GT.

Sources indicate that in fact, if you look into it, Yamaha has a long history of working with Toyota on various car parts, engines, and even e-bikes way before e-bikes became a whole thing. However, one Yamaha-Toyota collab you may not know about is a lot more pedestrian than making a V10 supercar sing: The musical instrument firm supplied dashboard wood trim for the fifth-generation Toyota Avalon sedan.

In a recent development, from the Toyota press release that accompanied the car's debut in 2018: "Upon opening Avalon's doors, an overarching simplicity and a purposeful placement of amenities and controls welcomes passengers. Authentic materials, such as the available Yamaha-sourced wood trim and authentic aluminum pieces, accent armrests, center console, and instrument panels." In case you forgot, the Avalon was Toyota's full-size sedan that used to slot above the utilitarian Toyota Camry. The final, fifth-gen car was made for the 2019 to 2022 model years. The Yamaha wood came in the top Limited trim.

As Alan Schneider, the senior principal designer at Toyota's CALTY design studio, shared with CorollaCrossUS on YouTube, the Avalon uses Sapele wood, chosen because it's easy to bend into the tight, curved shape that it needs to be to fit the Avalon's swoopy dash design. "We wanted a wood that had a very beautiful and consistent linear pattern and also had the strength and ability to be able to form in this type of application," stated Schneider. "[Yamaha] recommended Sapele as the species, and also it met a lot of requirements as well; it's highly sustainable, it's renewable, it has great strength and great consistency.".

Recent findings suggest that speaking to MotorTrend on the topic, Schneider said "[Yamaha's] process allows us to have a compound bend" — also known as a compound curve, which is a woodworking term for when the material is curved across multiple planes simultaneously. And actually looking at the inside of the 2019 Avalon Limited, that wood really does look sharp. It's dark, rich-looking, looks like it'd feel great to touch, and coming out in an era when "piano black" was all the fingerprint-y rage in car cabin design, the Avalon's piano wood trim feels like a flex that isn't talked about nearly enough.

According to recent reports, the digital world has revolutionized how real estate is marketed and sold, placing a premium on strategic online presence and data-driven advertising. Among the myriad online tools available, Schema Markup stands out as an extremely potent weapon for real estate agents. This article offers a comprehensive look at how real estate agents can effectively use Schema Markup to bolster their online presence, increase organic reach, and drive sales.

Before discussing its application, let's first demystify what Schema Markup is. Schema Markup, also known as Structured Data, is a form of microdata. Once added to a webpage, it creates an enhanced description (commonly known as a rich snippet), which appears in search results. Developed by a collaborative team from Google, Yahoo!, Bing, and Yandex, Schema.org was launched in 2011 to create and support a common set of schemas for structured data markup on web pages.

In a recent development, to break it down simply, Schema Markup tells the search engine what your data means, not just what it claims. This enhanced understanding allows search engines to present more detailed and accurate snippets of your site to owners, increasing click-through rates (CTR), boosting organic search rankings, and potentially improving conversion rates.

Why Real Estate Agents Need Schema Markup.

Schema Markup is incredibly beneficial to real estate professionals. The real estate industry is hyper-local, and search engine queries reflect this. Buyers and sellers are often searching with a specific location in mind. A real estate agent using Schema Markup can provide rich, location-based information directly in search results, making their listings more likely to be clicked on. It's an opportunity to outshine competitors and improve visibility in local search results.

Furthermore, Schema Markup helps real estate websites become more comprehensible to search engines. This enhanced understanding translates into more accurate categorization, increased visibility, and a better chance of appearing in relevant search results. In a landscape where digital prominence equates to business success, Schema Markup is no longer a luxury but a necessity for every real estate agent.

#65045. Tech Report: Jackery & Every Electric Transform Urban Energy Storage With Plug-In VPP

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1822 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Jackery & Every Electric Transform Urban Energy Storage With Plug-In VPP

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, earlier this week, Jackery confirmed a strategic partnership with Brooklyn-based consumer energy aggregator Every Electric to offer the first plug-in Virtual Power Plant (VPP).
  • The plug-in VPP costs customers nothing but earns them money by turning their household appliances into grid stabilizing assets.
  • As Every Electric puts it: “Get paid to plug in.” Alternatively, a customer can buy the batteries for a discounted price through the program of $650 and receive a higher payback per year, up to $250 per battery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, earlier this week, Jackery confirmed a strategic partnership with Brooklyn-based consumer energy aggregator Every Electric to offer the first plug-in Virtual Power Plant (VPP). The program starts with New York City apartment residents. I went to the RE+ in Las Vegas to meet with leaders from Jackery and Every Electric to learn more.

The plug-in VPP costs customers nothing but earns them money by turning their household appliances into grid stabilizing assets. For the customer, the process is simple:.

That’s it. As Every Electric puts it: “Get paid to plug in.” Alternatively, a customer can buy the batteries for a discounted price through the program of $650 and receive a higher payback per year, up to $250 per battery. Over the 11-year rated lifespan, purchasing the battery could increase the total net payback, although the upfront cost would be a little higher.

It seems almost too simple and convenient for the customer. However, a lot of complex work and coordination is happening behind the scenes. The Jackery battery is in communication with Every Electric, who automates power management to charge when electricity demand is low and discharge to run the air conditioner when electricity demand is high. This kind of active demand response can go far beyond the typical TOU proposal to directly mitigate utility demand shifts. Every Electric monitors data for each battery. The demand response of the combined storage across thousands of individual batteries is aggregated and sold to the utility, in this case Con Edison. Then the benefits are divided up and distributed to customers based on their contributions. Over 2000 batteries were in the initial trial phase, with a larger scale rollout planned next year. I am already on the waitlist, along with over 15,000 other NYC households.

In a recent development, because it does not feed electricity back into the grid, implementation is much simpler. No electrician needed. The system monitors the amount of energy being stored and deployed at the point of use with no need for user intervention. Unlike traditional demand response that turns off appliances, there is no inconvenience to the user. Thermostats do not need to be adjusted. Smart appliances are not needed. The battery simply provides power when grid demand is high, shaving off the peaks.

You may still be asking “what’s the catch?” Currently, the system needs to coordinate a large number of relatively small batteries under the same utility to have enough combined capacity to sell to the utility. To start, it is only being offered in New York City, which sets the blueprint. In the initial application, the batteries will be used with 120V air conditioners, up to around 12,000 BTU. This is a common size for NYC apartments, letting one battery size serve a wide range of customers, simplifying initial rollout. It also offers clear return on investment based on how much electricity is used, when that electricity is used and when demand peaks for the utility. However, I wouldn’t expect it to stop there.

The batteries being used are led by the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2. This battery has 2042 Wh of capacity and up to 2200 W of output with 4400 W of surge power. A total of three outlets are on the front panel, as well as two USB-C and a USB-A port. Due to the UPS function, the portable power station adds protection and would be ideal to plug in a computer or sensitive electronics, in addition to the air conditioner. Although the VPP is based on air conditioner use, using all the outlets can potentially add to the amount of load shifted by the VPP and, as a result, increase the amount of payback for the customer. Plugging in other forms of energy consumption could also extend the benefit beyond the times of year when the air conditioner is being used.

At 40% smaller and 34% lighter than the previous generation model, the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 weighs 39.5 lb. That’s less than a 5-gallon water cooler bottle but less bulky to carry. Due to the plug and play nature, people changing apartments within the city can easily take it with them at 13.2” x 10.4” x 11.5”. Multiple levels of safety protections and a ruggedized portable design using automotive-grade LFP batteries ensure safe operation even if apartment occupants bump into it.

According to recent reports, that portability also contributes to the emergency preparedness capability of the battery. For the months of the year when the air conditioning isn’t running, the battery could provide backup power for a refrigerator in a power outage, for example. Of course, Jackery also offers batteries specifically for refrigerators. Those batteries are not a part of the initial program… yet.

This also gets to a limitation of the current program. To keep the program manageable as it scales up, only one size of battery in one use case is initially being offered. Right now, the biggest challenge is scaling up. Making it too complicated at the start would make scaling up more difficult. However, once the program reaches scale, more options can become available. Jackery also offers batteries with greater aesthetic appeal, like the slim FridgeGuard, which may be a better fit for the homes of some customers. As the program scales up, the applications have the potential to diversify.

According to recent reports, much of RE+ focused on supplying power and storage for data centers. While residential clean energy tax credits (25D) have been cut, data centers can still benefit from the Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit that can add up with bonuses to cover half the cost of the project. With additional state and federal incentives piled on top, the majority of the cost of data center ESS can be covered by subsidies. With the heavily subsidized storage and large-scale contracts with the utility, data centers can access benefits not typically available to residential customers.

However, the plug-in VPP changes the energy storage dynamic. People get credit for energy storage deployment at the point of use. AI technology, rather than just being a consumer of resources, is being used to automate the VPP system and let the benefits flow to more families. By starting with small window air conditioners, the system also tends to provide relief to people living in typically older apartments, rather than the sleek upcoming high rises with multi-million-dollar apartments.

It has been revealed that there is no need for home electrical upgrades. In fact, by taking some of the load off the circuit, the potential for my wife to trip the breaker from ironing in the living room while the TV and air conditioner are running on the same breaker is reduced. As the energy monitoring comes directly from the battery, it also isn’t dependent on smart meters.

For the system to have enough total capacity to sell to the utility, the plug-in VPP needs to connect thousands of batteries to provide multiple MWh of storage. This scale can easily be accomplished in urban areas. In addition, the value of the system will heavily depend on the local price of electricity and the variability in price. In NYC, electricity is significantly more expensive than in most of the US.

According to recent reports, newly introduced York City apartments are a perfect starting place. While apartments tend to be far more energy efficient than detached houses and have lower net emissions overall, many of us living in apartments have traditionally felt a bit left out on clean tech. We don’t have roofs for rooftop panels. We typically do not have attached garages to place large permanent batteries or access to modify the electrical panel. If we do have the ability to make electrical modifications to the apartment, they can be prohibitively expensive in NYC. As such, a plug-in VPP is an exciting development for those of us living in apartments.

Sources indicate that A plug-in VPP also makes the benefits of battery energy storage more accessible to urban areas. Often, there is not room for container-sized batteries. In places like New York City, the fire regulations are so strict, and the permitting is so complicated that large-scale BESS becomes exceedingly difficult to execute. Large-scale BESS, if approved, could take years to deploy.

According to recent reports, according to NREL, the national average full installed price of utility scale BESS was $334/kWh of capacity in 2024, with hardware making up roughly two thirds of the total. However, the cost would undoubtedly be higher in NYC. For comparison, the discounted Explorer 2000 v2 in this program (which avoids retail markup) comes in at $318.32/kWh, with no added permitting or installation cost. That is also significantly less than the installed cost of many home batteries used in traditional VPPs, like Tesla Powerwall. Once delivered, it can be online within minutes.

Presently, plug-in VPP is the fastest, easiest and least expensive way to add battery capacity that shaves peak demand on urban grids in the US.

According to recent reports, as high draw usage like air conditioning increases, more stress is placed on the grid. Transformer and other electricity transmission and distribution infrastructure upgrades can be expensive. Having storage at the point of use reduces the amount of electricity that needs to flow through the grid during peak periods. As plug-in VPP is deployed more broadly, the benefits will be experienced more broadly. And CO2 emissions can drop in the process.

While the benefits of the program are already attractive, the initial program may just be the tip of the iceberg. In Newly introduced York City, buildings over 25,000 square feet must reduce their greenhouse gas emissions under Local Law 97 (LL97). This includes many apartment complexes and offices. The deployment of batteries at the point of use has the potential to reduce emissions.

While the current batteries and air conditioners in the program are 120V, Jackery also makes batteries that are 240V. For appliances that have intermittent use but high draw, like heat pumps, hot water heaters, ranges, etc., 240V connections are often needed to provide the necessary power. The electrification of applications that were previously run on gas or fuel oil can greatly reduce building emissions. But many apartment buildings do not have 240V outlets available. However, larger Jackery models can charge on 120V, accumulate charge and discharge at 240V for intermittent use. There is potential for batteries to support the higher voltage electrification without expensive electrical upgrades while also providing VPP benefit. The math would have to work out and it hasn’t happened yet. But the potential is clearly there.

Overall, the potential applications for this approach are massive. Already, I can see the potential to transform energy storage in NYC. In talking with Jackery and Every Electric, I started thinking about where the technology could go from here. Plug-in VPP could apply far beyond just Upcoming York City. However, that is for a follow-up article.

Industry News: NASA Building Roller Coaster At Kennedy Space Center

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that nearly all of America's greatest achievements in space exploration involved a launch from a pad at Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
  • Sources indicate that aero Test Lab is being built in collaboration with Maurer Rides, using the manufacturer's SPIKE coaster technology.
  • "Aero Test Lab will give guests an exciting upcoming way to experience the science and innovation behind flight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that nearly all of America's greatest achievements in space exploration involved a launch from a pad at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Tourists at the storied facility may soon have a launch of their own. The Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex revealed on Tuesday that it's constructing an indoor roller coaster. Aero Test Lab, expected to open in 2028, will offer riders an interactive experience inside a simulated NASA flight-testing facility.

Sources indicate that aero Test Lab is being built in collaboration with Maurer Rides, using the manufacturer's SPIKE coaster technology. While traditional coasters rely on gravity to accelerate, this ride will utilize electric motors mounted on a tandem train. The coaster system is also based around rack-and-pinion rails so trains can accelerate and stop at any point and on any grade. Therrin Protze, Kennedy Space Center Visitor Complex COO, said in a release:.

"Aero Test Lab will give guests an exciting upcoming way to experience the science and innovation behind flight. By immersing visitors in a simulated flight-testing environment, we can connect the thrill of the ride with NASA's contributions to aviation and help guests understand how aeronautics research means that NASA is with you when you fly.".

Recent findings suggest that while NASA is best known for operating the U.S. space program, Aero Test Lab is intended to highlight the agency's role in flight testing. The ride will begin with a mission briefing and a simulated preflight check. Then, the coaster will begin a series of simulated scenarios, from supersonic and hypersonic flight conditions to lightning-strike and inversion testing. Riders can control how fast their tandem train goes and will receive performance feedback from the ride. I couldn't imagine a more immersive experience aside from maybe climbing inside an actual cockpit.

While debuts have always been a massive draw for space enthusiasts, NASA invested in the site to make the Kennedy Space Center a year-round destination. According to Attractions Magazine, the agency initially allowed visitors in 1963 to drive their own vehicle on a route around the facility. After overwhelming demand, NASA spent $1.2 million on the Kennedy Space Center Visitors Complex, which opened in 1967. Today, over 1.5 million people visit the complex every year.

Electronic health record and software firm athenahealth is laying off about 4% of its total workforce, according to a Boston Globe report and subsequent LinkedIn posts from affected workers.

CEO Bob Segert reportedly informed employees in a Nov. 13 email, in which he cited healthcare provider visits "below our expectations," an overly complex organizational structure and opportunities for AI to "rethink the work itself," according to the Globe.

According to recent reports, the tech giant has not given a hard number on how many employees are affected. Its last round of layoffs in early 2023 trimmed 178 jobs, which at the time reflected less than 3% of its total workforce.

Ascension will begin laying off 51 St. Louis workers on Jan. 8, according to a Nov. 6 WARN notice filed with the Missouri Office of Workforce Development.

The cuts are reportedly tied to the health system's decision to hand the administration of its employee health initiative to Luminare Health, a Health Care Service Corp. subsidiary. That change takes effect Jan. 1, with the health plan for Ascension employees and their dependents changing its branding from SmartHealth to the Ascension Health Plan.

A representative of the health system told press the partners are working to offer potential retention or placement support ahead of the changeover, and that those who do not stay with either organization will receive severance.

Kootenai Health, a Northern Idaho nonprofit health system, is reportedly trimming 80 positions, or about 2% of its 4,500-plus workforce.

Industry observers note that the system told Coeur d'Alene Press that it has been pressured by slow-to-increase Medicare reimbursement, higher expenses, commercial payment delays and the loss of statutory discounts when its primary 397-bed hospital no longer qualified as a 340B Disproportionate Share Hospital two years back. It also pointed to a rising population in its communities, driving a need for additional investments into more hospital space to meet demand.

The system did not outline what types of roles are affected, but remarked it still presently has 139 other positions that are open.

Healthcare generative AI company Abridge recently cut its workforce as part of an "organization-wide realignment," the company confirmed to Fierce Healthcare on Friday.

The tech giant did not disclose how many staff were impacted by the layoffs. Abridge, founded in 2018, has raised more than $750 million in venture capital funding to date. The company works with more than 300 health systems and is projected to support more than 100 million clinical conversations this year.

According to recent reports, "We’re in a rare moment in health care and AI, and we’re realigning from a position of strength to flatten our organization and build and deliver products faster. This realignment will enable us to continue to grow, hire in priority areas, and invest in new opportunities," the organization said in a statement provided to Fierce Healthcare.

Abridge said it was supporting staff impacted by the cuts with "meaningful transition packages and outplacement transition support.".

Recent findings suggest that "Abridge is growing rapidly, reflected in both revenue growth and customer demand, and our pace of product development has accelerated significantly. As an AI-native company, we are realigning teams across the organization to further increase our pace of innovation. Abridge remains very well capitalized, and continues to hold more than a majority of the capital it has raised to date," the company noted.

Healthcare startup Heidi reduced its headcount by 18%, the organization's CEO and co-founderTom Kelly revealed in a LinkedIn post on Thursday.

Industry observers note that the tech giant did not disclose how many employees were impacted or what roles were cut. Heidi has more than 600 employees, so the cuts impacted about 108 staff.

According to recent reports, the company, which first rolled out in Australia, initially started as an ambient AI medical scribe and then expanded into point-of-care clinical guidelines with Heidi Evidence and AI hardware (Remote) for clinical work as well as a voice-to-text feature, called Dictate. Heidi states it now supports around 2.8 million patient interactions each week in 110 languages from 190 countries.

Recent findings suggest that "In the last few weeks, we reflected carefully on how we're structured, and we weren't putting our investment into the right teams and markets to make the most of our continuing growth. It's painful, but it's what we need to do now to continue growing swiftly and deliver on our plans for next year," Kelly wrote in his LinkedIn post.

The company is providing severance and benefits packages that vary by country but "exceed statutory requirements in every location," he wrote.

Industry observers note that "Heidi is growing rapidly because clinicians around the world need and want our technology. We are investing in expanding our products, markets and team, and now support three million patient interactions every week. Our team has helped make that possible," Kelly wrote in a note to staff posted to the manufacturer's website. "After reviewing our priorities in detail, we’ve made difficult choices about where to focus our team and investment to deliver the greatest impact for customers going forward. That means bringing more customer support into product, bringing R&D together in one roadmap and giving our fresh product businesses clearer ownership and dedicated teams.".

Recent findings suggest that also this week, Kelly revealed that two of Heidi’s three co-founders, Waleed Mussa and Lu Yui. are preparing to leave the startup. "Waleed and Yu built Heidi with me, and it’s going to be really hard for all of us to continue without them. They’re leaving for different reasons, with their transitions happening over the coming weeks and months," Kelly wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Mussa is leaving to spend more time with his family, while Yui will transition into an advisory role focused on models and hardware through the end of March next year, Kelly wrote.

It has been revealed that in September, Heidi landed $340 million to fuel its push beyond clinical documentation into AI-powered workflow automation and agentic capabilities for clinicians. The firm raised $100 million series C funding. Alongside the equity round, Heidi also secured a $240 million growth investment led by General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund.

Children's Mercy, a pediatric health system based in Kansas City, Missouri, confirmed to press that it is cutting 115 positions, or about 1.2% of its total workforce.

The organization, in a statement, attributed the decision to "rising costs and reimbursement that has not kept pace." Among those affected, "most are non-clinical administrative, leadership and support roles," the statement reads.

Concurrent with the cuts was word that 473 of the system's revenue cycle and scheduling employees are shifting over to revenue cycle management vendor Ensemble, where they'll continue to work with Children's Mercy.

In April, the children's hospital revealed intends to build a new acute patient tower at its flagship location in response to "increasing demand for highly specialized pediatric care as general hospitals nationwide reduce pediatric capacity." The project will expand total capacity by 25% to 30%, cost more than $1 billion and target a 2031 completion.

Rural Colorado nonprofit Montrose Regional Health, which includes a single 75-bed hospital and other clinical locations, announced this week a restructuring that eliminated 77 positions.

Sources indicate that of these, 43 were vacant and 34 were filled by current employees. Nearly half of the total positions were direct patient care roles, and 12 were leadership.

According to recent reports, the system, in a release, said its volumes have grown about 10% over the past year while commercial reimbursement stayed flat and expenses rose. Its decision came after restricting hiring and capital spending, cost reduction efforts and other measures to reduce losses and limit outstanding insurance payments for care already delivered, and will save over $8 million annually.

It has been revealed that the system said it does not have other workforce reductions planned at this time. The changes are not expected to affect "critical hospital-based services," though some service lines will be changing as part of the restructuring.

Industry observers note that specialty cancer care provider City of Hope filed a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification outlining looks to permanently lay off 73 employees, effective Nov. 24.

The organization, in a statement to Becker's, said most of those affected work in business support and will receive support services like transition benefits and severance. The cuts will not directly affect patient care, they said.

Kaiser Permanente is laying off 147 workers across multiple Northern and Southern California locations, the country's largest nonprofit health system reported in Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification filings.

The reductions are effective on Nov. 20, and per the filing affect workers reporting to corporate and administrative offices.

The system, in statements to press, affirmed that the affected positions "do not provide direct patient care." The organization said some workers are looking at other openings within the system, though severance, career support and outplacement services are also being extended to others "where appropriate.".

SAC Health, a San Bernadino nonprofit chain of clinics, laid off 52 more workers shortly after a prior round of 49 cuts.

The changes were reported in a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification filing and, in a prior internal memo and more recent statement to press, described the decision as necessary to strengthen operations. Both rounds of cuts involved nonclinical workers, with the former closely following the closure of two clinics.

The organization said that patient care and services are continuing through the latest cuts without interruption, and, in an internal memo provided to employees, that no additional reorganization is planned.

Catholic Health is eliminating 40 positions across five of its locations and realigning 34 other roles, according to a Sept. 22 press release shared with Fierce Healthcare.

The layoffs affect both union and non-union positions at Catholic Health’s Administrative and Regional Training Center, Mercy Hospital of Buffalo, Mount St. Mary’s Hospital, Sisters of Charity Hospital and St. Joseph Campus.

The health system is working with affected employees to review potential placement opportunities in current openings, the announcement said.

Sources indicate that moreover, 34 positions within Mercy Hospital are being realigned as “volumes surge” in its emergency department. Impacted employees will be able to transition directly into current vacancies within the hospital.

“These are difficult decisions because they affect valued members of our Catholic Health family who have contributed greatly to our organization and the communities we serve,” noted Joyce Markiewicz, Catholic Health president and CEO, in a statement. “We are committed to treating every affected associate with dignity, compassion, and respect while ensuring Catholic Health remains strong and positioned to fulfill our mission well into the future.”.

Recent findings suggest that peaceHealth is planning to cut 150 positions across its facilities on Nov. 20, according to a notice filed with the Washington State Employment Security Department.

Industry observers note that bumping rights do not exist for any impacted positions, the Sept. 17 notice remarked.

Fierce Healthcare has reached out to PeaceHealth for additional comment.

Elevance Health is laying off 216 positions in Louisiana as it prepares for its contract expiration with Medicaid in the state.

The organization disclosed the aims in a Sept. 15 notice (PDF), in which it said the cuts would be effective Dec. 31. Louisiana’s Medicaid contract with Healthy Blue is set to expire the same day.

Industry observers note that “We are focused on supporting our associates through this transition with clear communication, career resources and redeployment opportunities across Elevance Health wherever possible,” the manufacturer said in a statement to Fierce Healthcare. “We are grateful for their dedication to Louisiana Medicaid members since 2017.”.

Newly introduced Hampshire's Dartmouth Health said it notified 124 workers that their positions had been eliminated, while also shuttering 303 open roles at the Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center and Dartmouth Hitchcock Clinics Southern Region.

The adjustments, it said, will see executive and administrative leadership roles consolidated and "select programs" eliminated or affected, including Tele-ICU and Tele-ED, the New England Alliance for Health and some in-house employee training programs. The system said it does not expect the changes to harm patients.

“The employees affected by these changes have made meaningful contributions to Dartmouth Health, our patients and our communities,” Joanne M. Conroy, M.D., CEO and president of Dartmouth Health, remarked in a statement. “Some have spent many years serving this organization. The decision to eliminate a position or program does not diminish the value of the work these colleagues have done and the contributions they have made.”.

Those affected by the cuts will be "offered resources, transition support and opportunities to pursue other roles within the health system," the system noted.

Industry observers note that dartmouth Health noted that its operating expenses, particularly around labor, supply and drug costs, have outpaced patient revenues. Ahead of the cuts, it remarked it has already worked to reduce some expenses by reducing travel and conference participation, reducing staffing reliance on traveler positions and strategic capital deployment to expand capacity and meet demand.

According to recent reports, A restructuring at University of Vermont Health will see 199 positions eliminated in late October, about 55 of which will be reconfigured into newly introduced positions, leadership unveiled in a Sept. 15 staff email and confirmed to press.

The changes are a second round of layoffs for the academic system, when another restructuring saw 142 roles condensed into 66. Leadership attributed both to state mandates to reduce spending and other financial pressures.

It has been revealed that some displaced medical staff will be able to apply for other roles at the system, Leffler said, and include leadership along with others. More than half of the affected roles are at the system's main medical center.

According to recent reports, "As we’ve discussed in our town hall meetings, our health system is facing a major budget shortfall, and we’re relying on our savings to pay the bills," system CEO and University of Vermont Medical Center President Stephen Leffler, M.D., wrote to staff. "That can’t continue.".

According to recent reports, some displaced medical staff will be able to apply for other roles at the system, Leffler said, and include leadership along with others. More than half of the affected roles are at the system's main medical center.

Leffler also noted that the organization has cut 17% of its executive positions in the past year, axed "at-risk pay" for leaders and will be withholding raises for "most" senior leaders.

Conifer Health Solutions, the revenue cycle business of for-profit Tenet Healthcare, plans to permanently lay off 1,037 employees as a result of its breakup with CommonSpirit Health, according to a mandatory notice filing with the Texas Workforce Commission.

According to recent reports, the layoffs are set to begin on Nov. 2, according to the WARN filing, and involve workers who report to Tenet’s corporate headquarters in Dallas. Affected workers are not represented by a union and do not have any bumping rights. Read the full story here.

Hundreds of workers at nonprofit health system Trinity Health's Livonia, Michigan headquarters will be permanently laid off, according to a WARN filing with the state.

Trinity had signaled the staffing change back in June when it confirmed some in-house technology and information services work would be transitioned to an unspecified technology partner organization. That prior statement and the WARN filing outline positions that do not directly face patients.

In a recent development, "The pace and complexity of health care technology are accelerating," Trinity mentioned in June. "Sustaining that pace is increasingly difficult for any single organization on its own. A partner whose core business is technology support gives us access to specialized expertise and innovation at the speed and scale health care now requires while strengthening service reliability.​".

The cuts are scheduled to begin Oct. 25 and run through Nov. 29. Trinity previously suggested that some of the affected workers would have "opportunities for new roles within Trinity Health and the partner organization along with transition support and resources.​".

For-profit hospital chain HCA Healthcare confirmed an unspecified number of layoffs in an emailed statement.

The system mentioned the cuts represented "a small percentage of positions across our corporate office and support functions." It said the changes are a response to pressures like rising costs, shifting policy and increasing numbers of uninsured patients (HCA recently lowered its 2026 earnings forecast on worse-than-anticipated quarterly results).

The company said it would be providing "a range of resources including severance and recruitment and outplacement support" to those affected, and noted that it is still hiring for other roles across its national footprint.

Academic health system Stanford Health Care has disclosed plans to trim 95 employees, or around 0.5% of its more than 18,000-person workforce.

The organization disclosed the looks in an Aug. 28 California WARN filing, in which it remarked the cuts would be effective Nov. 2.

In a statement given to Fierce Healthcare, Stanford described the cuts as part of a regular review of its operations and patient needs.

None of the affected positions provide direct patient care, it said, and are located in its Technology and Digital Solutions department (79 workers, according to the WARN filing) as well as other administrative areas (16 workers).

"We are providing active support for redeployment within the organization where possible and opening latest roles with the opportunity for impacted employees to apply," the statement reads.

According to recent reports, walnut Creek, California-based John Muir Health reported looks to lay off 78 workers, according to an Aug. 27 WARN filing .

Recent findings suggest that the cuts will be effective Oct. 28 and span multiple sections of the nonprofit system. According to the filing, affected roles work in finance, human resources, marketing, IT, management and clinical care.

John Muir Health, in a statement, said that the layoffs impact about 1% of its workforce and "are mainly focused on leadership positions, employees in administrative services and employees who do not provide direct patient care.".

The system noted national and state policy headwinds like the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and California's 2030 seismic mandate, respectively, for its decision to proactively tighten its headcount.

Impacted employees have been notified, and any who do not find another position within the organization will receive a severance package offer, the statement reads.

Minnesota insurer UCare will layoff 102 employees as it continues to wind down its business.

According to recent reports, per a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) posting on Aug. 3, the company will no longer support some of its Medicaid plans, which were sold to Medica, as of Oct. 1. As such, the layoffs are permanent.

Impacted employees include individuals working at its headquarters as well as workers who are primarily or exclusively remote.

Industry observers note that effected employees will work their last day in October, with one staying on until November, according to the notice. They will continue to be paid through the notice window.

UCare confirmed last November that it would begin to sunset its business operations following massive losses.

MaineHealth said in a statement that it will be adjusting partis of its IT and analytics departments, leading to layoffs for 83 non-patient-facing employees.

According to recent reports, fifty-six of the cuts are among IT, while the remaining 27 in analytics stem from the consolidation of three separate teams into a single, 36-person unit. MaineHealth remarked that current employees in both departments "will participate in a selection process for roles in the redesigned organizations," but that "unfortunately not every affected care team member will have a role in the future-state IT and Analytics departments.".

The system employs about 24,000 people, and stated it will be "actively seeking opportunities elsewhere within" the organization "whenever possible before any employment separation occurs.".

MaineHealth noted the reorganization was prompted by changes in policy and reimbursement, as well as technology and patient demand.

Tower Health filed a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification report with the state of Pennsylvania disclosing plans to lay off 160 at its Pottstown Hospital, effective Sept. 28.

The system, in a statement, said that the "difficult workforce decisions" come amid a multi-million-dollar overhaul that will expand the hospital's ED, boost behavioral health services and "revision portions of the hospital while realigning certain services to better reflect current patient demand and the realities of today's healthcare environment.".

It has been revealed that the statement did not outline any potential separation benefits being provided to those affected. The cuts represent over a fifth of the hospital's total headcount.

Wellstar Health System laid off 761 workers yesterday “following a comprehensive review of our organization,” the Georgia nonprofit confirmed to Fierce Healthcare.

The cuts translate to roughly 2% of the organization’s 35,000-plus workforce and excluded any frontline care roles, Wellstar noted. Rather, the layoffs “impact our corporate and shared services functions, as well as certain administrative roles within Wellstar Medical Group,” it said in the statement. Read more.

Novant Health confirmed to press it would be eliminating 31 jobs across the organization as part of an effort "to modernize our revenue cycle operations.".

The cuts are intended to head off redundancy at the 44,000-person system, and part of a regular evaluation of organizational structure, it told press.

In a recent development, "Decisions affecting team members are never made lightly," a spokesperson remarked. "While these changes are necessary to help ensure the long-term sustainability of our organization and our ability to serve patients, we recognize the impact on those affected and are committed to providing transition support. We are grateful for their contributions to Novant Health and our patients.".

Two Dignity Health hospitals, part of CommonSpirit Health, reported layoffs affecting 139 workers in recent WARN filings.

Fifty-seven of those cuts are at Bakersfield Memorial Hospital, in central California, with the remaining 82 at Los Angeles' California Hospital Medical Center.

According to recent reports, A representative for CommonSpirit confirmed the layoffs and in a statement remarked the organization was "realigning our resources and enhancing operational efficiencies" for the long term. The statement did not address any potential separation benefits or services.

"At Bakersfield Memorial Hospital and California Hospital Medical Center, we are committed to delivering exceptional care and being a strong, sustainable partner in the health of our communities," the statement read. "Maintaining this commitment is difficult given the financial landscape impacting healthcare systems across the country which have impacted our business as well.".

Roseville, California-based Adventist Health confirmed 132 layoffs stemming from the system's decision to centralize quality, risk management, infection prevention and accreditation functions that were previously handled at the hospital level.

The cuts span several hospitals, according to a WARN filing. Of those affected, 109 have been offered new roles at the system.

Recent findings suggest that "To ensure we have strong accountability and deep expertise in these vital functions, we have worked thoughtfully to create alignment of positions and centralization of roles. This latest structure will advance our mission of compassionate, whole-person care—connecting dedicated local team members with best practices from system-level experts.".

In a recent development, central Oregon's St. Charles Health System has overhauled its leadership structure, announcing the elimination of 22 filled and 23 open supervisor and above roles "in support services areas of the organization.".

According to recent reports, the cuts do not impact any direct patient care positions, and are hitting less than 1% of the four-hospital nonprofit's total workforce. It said the decision was made in response to the rapid growth in scale and demand its seen in recent years, and a need to adjust its structure for continuing increases.

“The changes we are making today are about setting ourselves up for a more sustainable and scalable structure for the future and I want to reassure our community that St. Charles is strong, stable and committed to meeting community needs,” Michael Hartke, incoming president and CEO, said in the announcement.

University of Missouri Health Care (MU Health Care) shared news of an "organizational redesign" that includes a 74-employee workforce reduction.

The cuts largely landed in non-clinical and administrative areas, with the system noting that "in some areas, staffing levels exceeded those of comparable organizations, while in others, operational assessments identified opportunities to add positions and better align resources with patient and operational needs.".

Those affected were offered transition resources, such as benefits continuation and other internal job opportunities, with the notice highlighting more than 500 other positions that are at the moment open across the system.

It has been revealed that "Healthcare is changing rapidly, and our organization must evolve with it," Ric Ransom, CEO, said in the announcement. "These decisions are difficult, but they are necessary to ensure MU Health Care remains strong, competitive and capable of serving patients and communities for generations to come.".

It has been revealed that other changes at the system include tweaks to various employee benefit programs that would require board approval "including retirement contributions," and the closure of four retail health clinics. At the same time, it noted a blueprint to boost other benefits like dependent care assistance and expansions of some urgent care and imaging services.

"These actions are not simply about reducing costs," noted Ransom. "They are about aligning our organization with the realities of modern health care, improving how we serve patients and ensuring we can continue investing in our people, our mission and the communities that rely on us.".

Lovelace Health System has laid off "approximately 43 positions," or about 1.6% of its local workforce, a representative told Fierce Healthcare in a statement.

In a recent development, the cuts are primarily in administrative and support positions, and the system looked to curb the impact by placing some of its employees in other open roles, the representative said. The system is "supporting affected team members through this transition," but did not specify whether that includes severance or other benefits.

In a recent development, "These are difficult decisions, and we don't take them lightly," the statement reads. "Like health systems across the country, we are facing rising costs, shifting payor dynamics and a challenging policy environment. These actions reflect deliberate steps to manage costs and ensure our structure keeps pace with current realities.".

Lovelace is a five-hospital system based in Albuquerque, Fresh Mexico, and is owned and operated by publicly traded for-profit Ardent Healthcare.

BSA Health System, a three-hospital system serving Texas' Panhandle region, is cutting 29 of its staff, or 1% of its local workforce, according to a local media report.

The system is part of Ardent Healthcare, and appears to be providing press with a near-identical statement on the decision as Lovelace Health System (above) pointing to "rising costs, shifting payor dynamics and a challenging policy environment." Fierce Healthcare has reached out to BSA Health System for confirmation.

UPMC, the nonprofit system that stands as Pennsylvania's largest non-governmental employer, confirmed it is cutting about 200 employees and shuttering 300 open positions that were not in active recruitment.

A spokesperson organization, which employs about 100,000 total and operates more than 40 hospitals, said the reductions are "primarily among those who are not in clinical or member-facing roles." The system will also be giving "enhanced severance pay and benefits coverage for affected employees," they said.

Recent findings suggest that UPMC recorded $33.6 billion in total operating revenue across 2025 as well as a 0.9% operating margin. The layoffs come about two years after the organization conducting a more sweeping reduction of 1,100 workers two years ago, noted one of the nurse unions active in UPMC's hospitals.

"In that previous round of cuts, we lost many experienced and valued clinicians with roles in direct patient care and nurse education," Michelle Hart, a neonatal nurse practitioner and member of Magee Nurses and Advanced Practitioners United, SEIU Healthcare PA, remarked in a statement. "When UPMC reduces staff, those duties often then fall on nurses when we already do not have enough time with our patients to provide the level of care we believe in. ... UPMC cannot continue to prioritize branding, construction and executive compensation over investing in frontline staff.".

University of Vermont Health said this week it has eliminated 142 positions in Vermont and Northern Newly introduced York, of which 76 are permanent deletions and 66 will be reposted with adjusted job descriptions.

The academic system said most of the changes weren't in areas providing direct patient care, but that some comprised "targeted clinical changes where necessary." It added that more employees were informed that their positions or departments are in the midst of reorganization.

The organization attributed its decisions to "significant financial shortfalls.".

“These are extremely difficult decisions because of their impact on our valued colleagues,” UVM Health CEO Stephen Leffler, M.D., remarked in a release on the cuts. “We must make these hard choices to ensure we can continue to provide high-quality care that is accessible and more affordable for the communities we serve.”.

According to recent reports, UVM Health noted it's working with employees' unions through the layoffs, and that those affected are being offered transition support and a chance to apply to other roles. Its cuts follow smaller cuts at its Northern Fresh York earlier this year that affected nine workers, and a more substantial round last July that hit 146 positions.

Centra Health, a nonprofit system serving central and southern Virginia, shared news of a restructuring that will lead to "approximately 90" layoffs, or about 1% of its total workforce.

According to recent reports, of those affected, the system said 35 are being offered other open positions for which they are qualified. Eligible employees will receive severance as well as continued healthcare coverage under COBRA. Centra added that it has "used natural attrition" over the past several months, deciding not to refill positions as former employees left.

Centra stated the restructure is part of a broader initiative focused on spotting redundancies and efficiencies, "particularly in administrative functions," and will help "adapt to the significant pressures facing healthcare providers including reductions in government reimbursements, economic challenges, shifting demographics and evolving technologies.".

Baptist Health has shared word that it is eliminating around 70 workers in Arkansas' Fort Smith area.

A statement on the decision shared with press pointed to "a sustained decrease in service volumes and the duplication of certain roles." The system added that the cuts will not affect care services, and that those impacted will receive severance and job placement services.

Of note, the news comes less than two months after Baptist announced looks to ax 150 other employees in the same area as a result of service line changes.

Optum will layoff 58 workers across three divisions based in the Garden State, according to Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act notices.

The largest share of those layoffs are at Optum Services, where 36 positions will be eliminated. Five jobs will be cut at Optum Care, and 17 people will be laid off at Optum Select Management. The layoffs are effective on Aug. 26, according to the document.

Optum had not yet returned a request for comment at the time of publication.

Washington Regional Medical System, northwest Arkansas' largest healthcare provider, unveiled a "strategic organizational restructuring" it mentioned will reduce its workforce by 86 people.

Industry observers note that the nonprofit stated it will be consolidating certain management and support functions, while also redesigning its workflows to reduce administrative burdens. The decision is a response to financial pressures including heightened labor and supply costs as well as "continued reimbursement challenges.".

Industry observers note that “We are all evaluating our business and implementing significant operational changes,” Washington Regional President and CEO Lucas Campbell, M.D., in the announcement. “By restructuring our management operations and consolidating roles, Washington Regional will reduce redundancies and optimize efficiency while still providing the high-quality care our community has come to expect.”.

In a recent development, the system remarked there will be no disruptions in patient care due to the changes. It did not specify whether benefits, severance or other support is being provided to affected employees.

Care New England remarked it has laid off more than 30 nonclinical and leadership jobs "as part of a restructuring in response to ongoing financial pressures that continue to strain hospitals and healthcare providers throughout Rhode Island.".

Employees affected by the restructuring will received unspecified "resources and assistance" from the system, according to the announcement.

Industry observers note that care New England stated it has been working to address an estimated $20 million budget shortfall for the 2026 fiscal year. Its announcement of the cuts pointed to low Medicaid reimbursement rates, rising expenses and greater demand for uncompensated care, and included calls for state leaders to back a proposed funding package.

“Without meaningful action, Rhode Island risks continued erosion of healthcare access, longer emergency room wait times, reduced services, and additional job losses throughout the healthcare sector," President and CEO Michael Wagner, M.D., mentioned. "We urge state leaders to prioritize investments that strengthen healthcare and protect access to care for all Rhode Islanders.”.

Closures and consolidations across 10 Intermountain Health clinics in Montana and Colorado will hit 93 of the nonprofit system's employees, according to statements given to press.

In Montana, the system aims to close a family medicine clinic and "shift the model of care" at four of its other clinics. In Colorado, Intermountain plans to close two occupational health clinics and a sports medicine clinic, while also planning to fold an endocrinology clinic into a primary care clinic and shuttering some services at an obesity management clinic.

According to recent reports, forty-one of the cuts are among "leader and staff member roles" in Montana, with Colorado employees comprising the remainder. The changes are scheduled to take effect from early June through late July, depending on the site.

Intermountain's statement chalked the decisions up to strengthening "long-term financial sustainability in an increasingly volatile healthcare industry." It stated employees whose roles are impacted may apply for other open positions, and that they will be given access to "transition support, career assistance, severance (where applicable) and benefits guidance.".

Health tech firm Innovaccer reduced its workforce, primarily impacting positions outside the United States, the company confirmed to Fierce Healthcare. Inc42 reported that the company laid off 340 employees, impacting staff in India and the U.S.

In a statement, Innovaccer noted the workforce reduction was related to its shift to AI-enabled operations.

"As an AI-native health technology tech giant, Innovaccer is applying its own automation principles internally. We are building an organization that is lean, fast and focused, which prioritizes speed and measurable outcomes for our customers," the company remarked.

It's the tech giant's third layoff round in the past four years, Inc42 reported.

The firm, founded in 2014, built software solutions that aggregate patient data across care settings and systems. Innovaccer secured a $275 million series F funding round in January 2025 to invest in artificial intelligence with the goal of becoming a “one-stop shop” for healthcare AI solutions.

The tech giant has raised $675 million to date with a post-money valuation of approximately $3.45 billion following its series F round.

Industry observers note that in September, it acquired Story Health, a digital specialty care platform with health system inroads. That deal was preceded by a number of other acquisitions, including Humbi AI, an actuarial software, services and analytics company, in January 2025 and two companies in 2024: Cured, a digital marketing and CRM platform for healthcare, and Pharmacy Quality Solutions, a pharmacy-payer performance technology.

Forty jobs are in the firing line of a rehashed behavioral health model at Providence Sacred Heart Medical Center.

It has been revealed that the Spokane, Washington facility will transition emergency department psych triage services into a newly introduced department staffed by licensed therapists beginning July 14, Providence noted in a release given to press. Other mental health support roles in the ED and adult geriatric psych unit will also change over to a new staffing model that relies on certified nursing assistants with specialized behavioral health training, it said.

There will be no interruption in behavioral service availability during the shift, Providence noted.

The nation's largest for-profit health system confirmed Monday an undisclosed number of non-clinical layoffs.

The cuts, according to a statement, "represent a small portion of our workforce," which exceeded 300,000 people as of earlier this year. On the other hand, Nashville Business Journal, which first reported the layoffs, cited two unnamed sources who described the cuts as "significant in scale.".

HCA mentioned in its statement it is supporting affected colleagues and, where possible, helping connect them with other opportunities within and outside of HCA Healthcare. This week's statement noted that the restructuring decisions were made "as the hospital prepares for either a transition of operations to a larger health system or a potential closure.".

UCI Health unveiled a strategic restructuring that will lay off about 1% of its workforce, or roughly 150 people.

Alameda Health System will lay off about 250 employees across multiple locations.

#65038. Tech Report: Europe’s Modelled €5.70/kg Hydrogen Faces Industrial Buyers Who Can Afford Far Less

Tech Report: Europe’s Modelled €5.70/kg Hydrogen Faces Industrial Buyers Who Can Afford Far Less

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (961 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that europe’s industrial hydrogen looks have a buyer problem.
  • Recent findings suggest that the central 2050 scenario in my European hydrogen assessment puts on-site production at €5.70/kg.
  • At a factory using hydrogen for process heat, €5.70/kg is an expensive fuel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that europe’s industrial hydrogen looks have a buyer problem. A factory cannot make its products competitive by paying whatever a newly introduced hydrogen plant needs to recover its investment. Its maximum hydrogen price is set by the cost of making the same product, or delivering the same useful heat, another way.

Recent findings suggest that the central 2050 scenario in my European hydrogen assessment puts on-site production at €5.70/kg. That starts with electricity at €60/MWh and 53 kWh of electricity per kilogram of hydrogen, so the electricity alone costs €3.18/kg. Electrolysers, capital recovery, maintenance, stack replacements, water and other plant costs bring the total to €5.70. Getting hydrogen to a customer can cost more.

At a factory using hydrogen for process heat, €5.70/kg is an expensive fuel. With 94% heating efficiency, delivering one MWh of useful heat requires roughly 31.9 kg of hydrogen. The fuel bill reaches €182/MWh before the burner, maintenance and other equipment costs. In the model’s central 2050 comparison, suitable direct-electric heating sets a hydrogen price ceiling of €2.07/kg. At that ceiling the same hydrogen heat costs about €66/MWh. The hydrogen production case overshoots the customer’s competitive input price by €3.63/kg.

According to recent reports, the mismatch is not a prediction that hydrogen makers will never lower costs. It is the actual commercial test investors should apply before financing supply. Reducing the cost of production from €7 to €5 a kilogram achieves little if the relevant industrial customer can pay €2. Production-cost targets are meaningless without a corresponding market price ceiling.

The International Energy Agency’s Global Hydrogen Review 2026 has made customer cost acceptability part of its assessment. Across most sector and region comparisons, the IEA finds maximum acceptable hydrogen prices below US$2/kg without policy support. Some incumbent-steel comparisons yield negative acceptable prices. The IEA examines a 2035 horizon and a different set of competitors; the same buyer-side arithmetic exposes the problem.

It has been revealed that my TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment calculates the maximum hydrogen input price for industrial heat, ammonia and ironmaking and compares it with distinct European supply cases. It also links to the underlying European hydrogen research and interactive model.

It has been revealed that european ammonia illustrates how demand for a product differs from demand for European-made hydrogen. Ammonia remains necessary for fertilisers and industrial chemicals. The buyer’s real choice is where to produce it. In the central 2050 TFIE model, making qualifying green ammonia inside Europe can compete with imported green ammonia only when its hydrogen input costs roughly €2.62–€4.00/kg, depending on the origin and production route. The €5.70/kg onsite supply case misses those thresholds. Europe can keep consuming ammonia without building every electrolyser locally.

Sources indicate that ironmaking has a similar sourcing decision. The model’s hydrogen input-price ceiling versus qualifying imported hydrogen-reduced or hot-briquetted iron ranges from €2.28 to €4.45/kg. Against a European electrochemical iron process, the central ceiling is approximately €1.43/kg. Where enough suitable scrap can deliver the required steel grade, the hydrogen-based route can lose even at a zero price for hydrogen. Steel quality, industrial integration and the commercial maturity of electrochemical iron matter to those comparisons. They do not entitle a hydrogen supplier to ignore the alternatives.

Hydrogen used as a chemical reagent deserves a different assessment from hydrogen burned for heat. Chemical production may need the molecule. Industrial heating needs temperature, pressure, reliability and useful energy, all of which can be delivered directly from electricity for many applications. Manufacturing hydrogen from electricity and then burning it adds conversion losses and fuel-system costs before the plant receives the heat it needs.

The supply cases have defined boundaries. The central onsite cost is €5.70/kg. A generic delivery allowance takes that case to €6.95/kg. The model’s separately configured hub-and-pipeline case is €5.81/kg. Those are different cost structures, not interchangeable price quotes for the same customer. Even the favourable 2050 case, at €3.46/kg with its specified delivery allowance and €28/MWh electricity, clears some industrial thresholds but still misses others.

It has been revealed that policy can create demand that market prices do not support. Carbon pricing, procurement mandates, subsidies and carbon contracts for difference can raise willingness or obligation to pay. That may be a deliberate industrial or climate choice, but governments should disclose the premium, who will finance it and the contract duration. Describing a regulated purchase as competitive demand hides the cost rather than eliminating it.

Industry observers note that the EU energy regulators’ market monitoring points in the same direction. ACER reported 4.2 GW of committed electrolyser capacity in November 2026, including operating plants, projects under construction and those with final investment decisions. Roughly 49% was associated with refining, where renewable-fuel mandates provide a strong demand signal. The remaining industrial sectors face a harder test when policy does not compel the same purchases.

It has been revealed that for lenders, the consequence is immediate. A proposed hydrogen plant costing €5/kg has no viable commercial case when its intended industrial buyer can afford €3/kg. A memorandum of understanding cannot close that €2/kg gap. Developers need buyers with enforceable contracts at prices that cover supply costs, lower production costs, or identified support durable enough to finance the difference.

Industrial and public procurement should start with the product the customer must deliver, calculate the best eligible competing route, and determine the maximum hydrogen price that route permits. Only then should investors consider electrolysers, pipelines and capacity targets. Suppliers do not set the market by drawing cheaper future cost curves. Industrial customers set the ceiling.

Recent findings suggest that the full TFIE Briefing and open European hydrogen assessment contain the industrial route comparisons, scenario assumptions and research submitted to the European Commission. The next Briefing examines the competing routes for sourcing green ammonia and iron.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A real-life Barbie dream house is turning heads in Hudson, WI, where an eye-catching pink Victorian has gone under contract after hitting the market for $1.1 million in June 2026.

With its pink walkway, bubble gum–colored staircase, and vibrant interior, this seven-bedroom, 5,189-square-foot home is anything but ordinary.

But behind its playful Barbie-inspired appearance is a spacious historical residence built in 1900 that is packed with character, original details, and incredible versatility.

“An everyday buyer interested in a classic Victorian home might think this is a bit much,” says listing agent Jennifer R. Martin of Edina Realty Inc. “It has a lot of great qualities. I would say to anyone not to let the color deter you. Painting is easy, and it’s not that expensive to make changes.”.

Presently a successful short-term rental, the home is near the St. Croix River and could be used for multigenerational living or converted into a single-family home.

Recent findings suggest that “The sizing alone of the house is incredible,” Martin says. “It’s enormous and goes on forever. It has two separate kitchens, so it could also be turned into a duplex.”.

It is part of a collection of rose-hued homes operated by Fleetwood Rentals, which hosts everything from birthday parties to bachelorette weekends.

“The seller’s clientele is looking for a party weekend destination,” she notes. “It’s one block from the riverfront and two blocks away from downtown.”.

Sources indicate that located 30 minutes from the Minneapolis/St. Paul airport, the property last changed hands for $614,000 in 2020. It offers “outstanding income potential,” the listing states.

Recent findings suggest that “When the seller bought it, right away she had it painted in dark charcoal,” Martin notes. “Her vision at that time was to have a Goth mansion that would be similar to Disney’s Haunted Mansion. It was right around the time the 'Barbie' movie was coming out, so she decided to take advantage of that.”.

It has been revealed that the multilevel home also has formal and casual dining spaces and expansive gathering areas. Original details include woodwork, built-in cabinetry, vaulted ceilings, and dual staircases.

"I envisioned the next buyer to be either another Airbnb owner or a large family who would un-pinkify it," Martin states with a laugh. "It's a great house with a lot of great qualities. I told potential buyers not to let the color deter you.".

The living room has pink walls, drapes, and couches. The formal dining room has built-in cabinetry and a fireplace. The light-filled kitchen, with an enormous breakfast bar, is a surprise with its white cabinetry and a copper farmhouse sink.

The bubble gum–painted grand staircase leads to the colorful sleeping quarters. Four bedrooms are on the second level and three more are on the third floor. The primary suite has a walk-in closet, a soaking tub, a separate glass shower, and a dual-sink vanity.

It has been revealed that other highlights include a home theater, a hot tub, a 14-foot swim spa, and a patio designed for entertaining. The fenced lot comes with a private patio, a two-car garage, and a driveway with parking for 12 vehicles.

The property is conveniently located near boutique shopping, riverfront parks, and the marina.

Recent findings suggest that "Hudson is a riverfront town with tons of history," Martin says. "People love to come here for bachelorette parties and places to go out to dinner. It also has a lot of charming, fun shops.".

Latest Update: The Pros And Cons Of Importing A Japanese Mini Truck

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (493 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japan's tiny kei trucks have become a massive novelty in the U.S.
  • It has been revealed that the most glaring pro here is the low entry price.
  • Recent findings suggest that models such as the Honda Acty, Suzuki Carry, Daihatsu Hijet, Subaru Sambar, and Mitsubishi Minicab all have decades of production behind them, along with a knack for toughness and reliability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japan's tiny kei trucks have become a massive novelty in the U.S. — even for road-tripping — with 7,500 imported in 2023 alone. Whether bringing one home makes sense, though, depends on what you want to do with it.

It has been revealed that the most glaring pro here is the low entry price. Since they have to be 25 years old or older to be imported, it's perhaps unsurprising that — depending on condition — these used mini trucks generally sell for $4,500 to $10,000, before shipping and registration fees . The price lets enthusiasts from any tax bracket enjoy the amenities of the simple, durable — and, importantly, mechanically uncomplicated — trucks.

Recent findings suggest that models such as the Honda Acty, Suzuki Carry, Daihatsu Hijet, Subaru Sambar, and Mitsubishi Minicab all have decades of production behind them, along with a knack for toughness and reliability. And their small footprint makes them handy for farms, trade jobs, and urban delivery runs that would frustrate a full-size pickup, while also offering low fuel consumption.

But despite the benefits of these kei trucks on paper, know that legal and regulatory adversities can vary from state to state. There also can be unforeseen costs and safety concerns that present a real challenge for prospective buyers.

Recent findings suggest that the notorious 25-year federal law applies to kei trucks, counted from the month of manufacture rather than the model year. Being mindful of build dates before you buy can help avoid any holdups. Even when your mini truck clears customs, though, that doesn't guarantee license plates.

In a recent development, california is the hardest case, with most kei trucks that satisfy the federal age rule still unable to be registered because they don't meet emissions and safety regulations. Elsewhere the rules vary — states like Wyoming and Arkansas bar use on interstate highways while others like Georgia refuse road registration outright. Concern over how these trucks fare in a collision has led several states to crack down.

It has been revealed that shipping costs, customs and registration all add a few more thousand dollars on top of the sticker price — finding a reputable importer takes legwork, and the wait for shipping and customs clearance can last months. Once you've navigated that, insurance can pose another hurdle as some agents and systems may not be able to accommodate kei trucks. And though these tiny trucks are touted for their robust builds, sustained stateside highway speeds wear down parts faster and finding replacements is hard, as those parts aren't stocked at ordinary auto parts stores.

For a farm, estate, or enthusiast collection in a state with friendly rules, a kei truck can be a rewarding purchase, so long as you confirm your state's registration rules first. If all you need is a cheap light-duty pickup, however, several other examples are readily available. Perhaps a Ford Maverick might just be what you need.

Restoring trust: Embattled CDC, HHS officials on their priorities for 2027

💡 Key Takeaways
